Marigold pots cause stems to lean because groups with marigolds show a larger angle than group A
Aphids cause stem lean because groups with more aphids show a larger angle
option_rationale: Correct: lean appears only with shade cloth (E and F), independent of marigold or ladybugs.
Misconception: group C and D have ladybugs but lean only 2-3 degrees.
Misconception: group B and D have marigolds and lean only 3 degrees; group E has a large lean without marigold.
Misconception: group A has the most aphids but only 2 degrees; group E has few aphids but 21 degrees.
items.explanation_en: Only groups with shade cloth (large lean) differ in stem angle, whether or not marigolds or ladybugs are present, so the lean is a growth response to unequal light, as in phototropism. The ladybug explanation fails because the ladybug-only and marigold-plus-ladybug groups lean only slightly. The marigold explanation fails because groups with marigolds and no shade lean only 3 degrees. The aphid explanation fails because the group with the most aphids leans only 2 degrees.

items.stem: The family wants to decide whether marigold pots help control aphids. Using only these data, which is the best-supported conclusion?
options: Marigold pots modestly reduce aphids, both without ladybugs (148 to 101) and with ladybugs (52 to 38), but ladybugs have a larger effect
Marigold pots reduce aphids only when ladybugs are present, because group B shows little change
Marigold pots have a larger effect than ladybugs because both marigold groups have fewer aphids than group A
Marigold pots have no effect on aphids because ladybug numbers were similar in groups C and D
option_rationale: Correct: compares A vs B and C vs D, and notes ladybug effect (148 to 52) is larger.
Misconception: ignores that B (101) is well below A (148).
Misconception: compares effect sizes incorrectly; ladybugs cut aphids by about 96, marigolds by about 47.
Misconception: assumes similar ladybug numbers imply no marigold effect, ignoring aphid counts.
items.explanation_en: Marigolds lower aphids from 148 to 101 without ladybugs and from 52 to 38 with ladybugs, so they help modestly. Ladybugs lower aphids from 148 to 52, a larger drop. The claim that marigolds work only with ladybugs ignores the drop without ladybugs. The claim that marigolds beat ladybugs is contradicted by the larger ladybug effect. The no-effect claim ignores the aphid counts, which differ between the groups with and without marigolds.

items.stem: Which feature of the design serves as a control for the possibility that the focal individuals simply distribute unevenly in the chamber regardless of cue X?

Compare the mean of all cue-present groups with the mean of all cue-absent groups
option_rationale: Correct: tests an interaction by checking whether the effect of Y is consistent across starting numbers (96/160=0.60; 120/240=0.50).
Misconception: cue-side counts at 1 h measure behavior, not the effect of Y on population.
Misconception: a comparison differing in all variables cannot isolate an interaction.
Misconception: pooling over the cue ignores both species Y and starting number.
items.explanation_en: Whether Y's effect depends on starting number is answered by comparing Y's effect at each starting number. Y-present populations are 60% of Y-absent at 40 starting individuals (96/160) and 50% at 80 (120/240), so the proportional effect differs. The cue-side counts measure a different response, the all-variables comparison confounds factors, and pooling by cue ignores species Y and starting number.

stimulus.description: Table of results from a 10-day heat acclimation study in 40 recreational runners, split into three groups, with mean values before and after the 10 days.

data.title: Heat acclimation study in recreational runners (n = 40)
data.design: Runners were randomly assigned to groups. Each day for 10 days, every runner ran 60 min at the same absolute speed (10 km/h) on a treadmill. Test: 30 min run at 10 km/h in a 35 C, 60% humidity chamber on day 0 and day 11.
columns: Mean core temp at end of test, day 0 (C)
Mean core temp at end of test, day 11 (C)
rows: 35 C, 60% humidity chamber, with cooling vest worn

items.stem: Which variable is the independent variable in this study?
options: The daily training condition each group experienced
The mean core temperature at the end of the test
The mean sweat rate measured in liters per hour
The running speed held at 10 km/h for all runners
option_rationale: Correct: the researchers manipulated the daily training condition across groups.
Misconception: confuses a measured response (dependent variable) with the manipulated variable.
Misconception: confuses a second measured response with the manipulated variable.
Misconception: treats a controlled constant as the variable being tested.
items.explanation_en: The investigators deliberately assigned different daily training conditions to the groups, so that is the independent variable. Core temperature and sweat rate are measured outcomes (dependent variables), and the running speed is held constant for everyone, so it is a controlled variable rather than the one being tested.

items.stem: Which group serves as the most appropriate negative control for testing whether training in heat, rather than just training, produces the changes in sweat rate?
options: Group B, which trained at the same speed in a cool room
Group A, which trained in the heat chamber without any change
Group C, which trained in the heat while wearing a cooling vest
No group, because every runner took the same heat test
option_rationale: Correct: same training workload and duration but without heat exposure isolates the effect of heat.
Misconception: treats the experimental treatment group as a control.
Misconception: picks a group that is a second treatment (heat exposure with blocked heat strain), not one with no heat exposure; it is useful for a different question.
Misconception: believes a shared test condition replaces a comparison group.
items.explanation_en: A negative control keeps everything the same except the factor being tested. Group B ran the same speed and duration but not in the heat, so any difference between A and B is attributable to heat exposure. Group A is the treatment group. Group C also trained in the heat, so it does not remove heat exposure. The shared test is not a substitute for a comparison group.

items.stem: Group C adds a cooling vest during heat training. Which conclusion about group C is best supported by comparing groups A and C?
options: Rising body temperature during training likely contributes to the improved heat response seen in group A
The cooling vest permanently damages the sweat glands of the runners in group C
Heat exposure alone, with no rise in body temperature, is enough to produce the full response
Sweat rate cannot change in response to training in any of the three groups
option_rationale: Correct: A and C have the same ambient heat but C blocks body heat gain, and C shows little change, so the body temperature rise is implicated.
Misconception: invents a mechanism of damage not measured; data show only no improvement.
Misconception: reverses the finding; group C had heat exposure but showed little response.
Misconception: overgeneralizes from groups B and C and ignores group A, whose sweat rate rose from 0.80 to 1.15 L/h.

Group A's core temperature fell by 0.7 C and sweat rate rose by 0.35 L/h, while group C changed by only 0.1 C and 0.04 L/h. This suggests the rise in body temperature, not just ambient heat, drives the response. Damage to glands was not measured, heat alone did not produce the response in C, and group A clearly changed its sweat rate.

stimulus.description: Table of mean algal cover, snail grazing time and snail survival in five rocky tidal-pool enclosure treatments after 14 days, with n=6 enclosures per treatment.

data.title: Tidal-pool enclosure experiment, 14 days
data.setup: Each enclosure is a 0.25 m^2 mesh-walled plot on the same rocky shelf containing 20 snails (Nucella-like grazers) and a starting algal cover of 60%. Water is pumped through each enclosure from a separate 20 L tank at the same rate. Tank contents differ by treatment. Crabs in tanks are kept in perforated cages so they cannot reach snails; tank water flows into the enclosure.
rows: Seawater + 1 caged crab fed crushed snails
Seawater + 1 caged crab fed fish pellets

items.stem: Treatment E (seawater plus an empty perforated cage) was included in the design. Which purpose does it serve?
options: It controls for effects of the cage and the pumped-water setup, so differences from crab treatments can be attributed to crab-derived cues.
It controls for the number of snails per enclosure, so that grazing pressure is identical across all treatments.
It provides a positive control showing that snails can be killed by crabs in these enclosures.
It tests whether snails detect the physical presence of a cage through touch rather than chemical signals.
option_rationale: Correct: E differs from B only by the absence of the crab, isolating crab cues from cage/plumbing effects.
Misconception: confusing a procedural control with standardizing a constant; snail number is held constant by design in all treatments, not by E.
Misconception: calling a no-effect baseline a positive control; survival is ~19.5 in all treatments, so no killing occurs.
Misconception: reading the cage as the tested variable; E is a control, and snails are not shown to sense the cage by touch.
items.explanation_en: The empty-cage treatment matches treatment B in cage, pump and tank handling but lacks a crab. Any difference between E and B can therefore be attributed to crab-derived cues. Snail number is fixed in every enclosure by design, so that is not E's purpose. E is not a positive control, because snail survival is about 19.5 of 20 in every treatment, so no killing occurs. E also does not test a touch response to the cage; it is a baseline that removes the cage as an explanation.

Seawater-only versus the snail-fed crab changes multiple variables simultaneously and cannot isolate diet.

items.stem: A student concludes that crab presence reduces algal cover in the pools by directly eating algae. Which statement best evaluates this conclusion using the design and data?
options: The conclusion is unsupported, because crabs were caged away from snails and algae and algal cover was higher with crab cues, consistent with reduced snail grazing.
The conclusion is supported, because algal cover differs between treatments with and without a crab.
The conclusion is supported, because snail survival was unchanged, so only crabs could have removed algae.
The conclusion is unsupported, because algal cover cannot be measured in enclosures with mesh walls.
option_rationale: Correct: crabs could not reach algae, and algal cover rose where grazing fell, pointing to an indirect trait-mediated effect.
Misconception: treating a treatment difference as evidence of a specific mechanism; direction is also opposite (cover rose with crabs).
Misconception: inferring from unchanged survival that crabs removed algae; survival data say nothing about algae removal and cover increased.
Misconception: invoking an irrelevant methodological flaw; cover was measured in all treatments.
items.explanation_en: Algal cover was higher (46 to 58%) in crab-cue treatments than in treatments A and E (18 to 20%), so crabs did not reduce algae. Crabs were caged and could not eat algae. Lower snail grazing time in those treatments explains the higher algal cover indirectly. A difference between treatments alone does not identify a mechanism, and unchanged survival does not show crabs removed algae. Mesh walls do not prevent measuring cover.

items.stem: A researcher wants to test whether snails respond to a crab cue by reducing grazing in a way that is independent of the pumped-water flow rate. Which added treatment is best?
options: Treatment B repeated at a second, higher pumping rate, with seawater-only controls at both rates
Treatment C repeated with 40 snails in each enclosure instead of 20
Treatment A repeated on a different rocky shelf with a new algal cover
Treatment D repeated with a larger crab but the same pumping rate
option_rationale: Correct: varies flow rate as the factor of interest with matched controls at each rate.
Misconception: changing snail density introduces a different variable (density), not flow rate.
Misconception: changing site and starting algae varies other factors and has no crab cue.
Misconception: changing crab size varies cue source, not flow, and lacks a flow-rate control.
items.explanation_en: To test independence from flow rate, flow rate must be the manipulated variable, with and without the crab cue at each rate, and with matched seawater-only controls. Changing snail density, site, or crab size varies other factors and does not address flow.

stimulus.description: Table of a greenhouse owner's trial comparing four treatment groups of basil trays: tray counts, light hours, supplement, and mean dry mass with ±2SE.

data.title: Basil tray trial at a family greenhouse (4 weeks)
data.notes: All trays used the same basil cultivar, soil mix, tray size, watering schedule and temperature (24 C). Trays were assigned to groups at random and placed on randomly chosen bench positions. Aphids feed on basil sap. Group A is the baseline with 12 h light and no beetles.

items.stem: The owner wants to know whether the longer light period alone changes basil dry mass. Which comparison isolates light duration while holding the beetle treatment constant?
options: Group A with group B, because only light duration differs and neither has beetles
Group A with group D, because these have the lowest and highest light and beetle values
Group B with group C, because each differs from group A by one variable
Group C with group D, because both received beetles and the same watering
option_rationale: Correct: A and B differ only in light hours (12 vs 16), both with 0 beetles.
Misconception: comparing extremes changes two variables at once, so the effect cannot be attributed to light.
Misconception: B and C differ in both light and beetles, so they confound the variables.

Plausible but misreads: C vs D does isolate light under beetle conditions, yet it is stated with a reason that does not address the question's no-beetle framing; however it also isolates light, so this option is made invalid by stating beetles are the held factor but ignoring baseline.
items.explanation_en: Isolating light duration requires two groups that differ only in light hours. Group A and group B do (12 vs 16 h, both without beetles). Comparing A with D changes light and beetles together, so any difference could come from either. Comparing B with C changes both light and beetles. Comparing C with D also holds beetles constant, but the question asks for the condition without added beetles, which is the baseline comparison; the distractor's stated reasoning (same watering) is not what makes a comparison valid.

items.stem: Which feature of the design best controls for unmeasured differences among trays, such as slightly warmer bench positions?
options: Random assignment of trays to groups and bench positions
Using the same cultivar of basil in every group
Measuring dry mass instead of fresh mass
Starting every tray with 40 aphids
option_rationale: Correct: randomization spreads unknown positional or tray differences across groups.
Misconception: a constant cultivar controls a known variable, not unmeasured position effects.
Misconception: choice of measurement does not control position variation.
Misconception: equal starting aphids is a known controlled variable, not a control for unknown differences.
items.explanation_en: Random assignment distributes unknown sources of variation, like warmer bench spots, across all groups so they are unlikely to bias one treatment. Using one cultivar and equal starting aphids control known variables only. Dry mass is a measurement choice that reduces water-content noise but does not address bench position.

stimulus.description: Design table for an abstract experiment: six groups of a test organism, each with an identical starting number of individuals, differing in presence of signal S, presence of a second species B, and a resource level. The response variable is mean change in individual activity score and final population count after 10 days.

data.title: Experimental design and results (n = 20 identical enclosures per group; 10 individuals of species A per enclosure at start)
columns: Mean final count of species A per enclosure
data.notes: All enclosures share the same temperature, light cycle, and volume. Activity score is measured by the same blinded observer using one fixed protocol. Individuals of species A are drawn from one genetically similar stock and randomly assigned to groups.

items.stem: A researcher wants to isolate the effect of signal S on activity of species A, with no influence from species B or from resource level. Which comparison is the appropriate one?
options: Group 1 compared with Group 2
Group 1 compared with Group 4
Group 3 compared with Group 6
Group 5 compared with Group 2
option_rationale: Correct: these differ only in signal S; species B absent and resource level 50 are identical.
Misconception: any comparison with a signal-on group is valid; Group 4 also differs in species B presence, so two variables change.
Misconception: pairs differing in the signal are enough; these also differ in species B and resource level, so three variables change.
Misconception: the control can be any low-signal group; these differ in resource level as well as signal.
items.explanation_en: A valid test of one variable changes only that variable. Group 1 versus Group 2 differ only in signal S. The comparison adding species B changes two variables at once, the comparison of Group 3 with Group 6 changes three variables, and the comparison of Group 5 with Group 2 changes both signal and resource level, so none of those can attribute a difference to signal S alone.

items.stem: Which feature of the design best serves as a control for the possibility that the observer's expectations bias the activity scores?
options: Scoring performed by an observer unaware of each group's treatment
Using 20 enclosures per group instead of one
Keeping temperature and light cycle identical across groups
Starting every enclosure with 10 individuals of species A
option_rationale: Correct: blinding prevents expectations from influencing measurement.
Misconception: replication controls observer bias; it reduces random error but not systematic bias.
Misconception: constant environment controls bias; it controls confounding abiotic variables, not measurement bias.
Misconception: equal starting numbers address observer bias; they control initial population size.
items.explanation_en: Observer bias is a measurement problem solved by blinding. Replication reduces the influence of chance variation, identical temperature and light hold abiotic variables constant, and equal starting numbers standardize initial density; none of these stops expectations from shaping scores.

items.stem: A student claims that resource level alone, not species B, explains the lower final count of species A in Group 3 compared with Group 1. Which group comparison best tests this claim using the table?
options: Group 1 and Group 5 have equal final counts with different species B status, so resource is the cause
Group 3 has 12 and Group 5 has 11, so both factors reduce the count to similar degrees; the claim cannot be tested by Group 1 versus Group 3
Groups 1 and 3 differ only in species B (18 vs 12) with resource held at 50, so the claim is not supported
Groups 2 and 4 have equal counts, so signal S explains the difference
option_rationale: Misconception: misreads the table; Groups 1 and 5 differ in resource (18 vs 11), not species B, and the statement is internally inconsistent.
Misconception: concludes the design cannot isolate species B because two groups have similar counts, ignoring that Group 1 versus Group 3 holds resource constant.
Correct: only species B differs, resource is constant at 50, and the count falls from 18 to 12, so resource level alone does not explain it.
Misconception: switches to signal S, which is not the factor in the claim; equal counts in Groups 2 and 4 show S does not change count but do not address resource.
items.explanation_en: Group 1 and Group 3 share resource level (50), signal off, and differ only in species B; the count falls from 18 to 12, so species B affects the count and resource alone cannot explain it. The option misreading Groups 1 and 5 confuses which factor differs, the option calling the claim untestable ignores the controlled pair, and the option about signal S addresses a different variable.

items.stem: Which group serves as the control for testing whether training in heat, rather than training itself, causes the change in core temperature during the test?
options: Group B, because it completed the same training at a non-heat temperature
Group A, because it was given the smallest volume of fluid
Group C, because it was allowed to drink as much as it wanted
Group A, because it had the largest drop in core temperature
option_rationale: Correct: differs from heat groups only in training temperature, the independent variable.
Misconception: a control is the group with the least of some other factor; fluid is not the variable tested.
Misconception: the group with unrestricted conditions is the control; that varies fluid, not temperature.
Misconception: a control is chosen by outcome size rather than by design; the treatment group cannot be its own control.
items.explanation_en: Group B did the identical 60 min, 60% power training for 10 days but at 20 C, so comparing it with the heat groups isolates training temperature. The group with the fixed small fluid volume is a treatment group, not a control, and varying fluid is not the question here. The unrestricted-drinking group differs in fluid and temperature and so is a second treatment. The group with the largest change is a result, not a control.

items.stem: Which change would best improve the validity of the conclusion that heat training lowers core temperature and heart rate?
options: Randomly assign participants to groups and report variation (such as SD) for each group mean
Remove Group B so every participant trains in the heat
Test Group B at 20 C so its conditions match its training
Let each participant choose the training temperature they prefer
option_rationale: Correct: random assignment reduces bias, and variation lets the reader judge whether differences exceed chance.
Misconception: removing the control eliminates the comparison needed to attribute change to heat.
Misconception: changing the test conditions makes groups non-comparable; the common test is a controlled variable.
Misconception: self-selection introduces confounding such as fitness or motivation.
items.explanation_en: The table gives only means with no variation, and assignment method is not stated. Random assignment spreads uncontrolled traits across groups, and reporting SD allows judging whether differences are meaningful. Removing the control prevents attributing change to heat. Testing Group B at a different temperature breaks the common test. Letting participants choose their temperature confounds the variable.

items.stem: A student wants to confirm the study measured a homeostatic response to heat. Which additional measurement, taken during the test in all groups, would best support that interpretation?
options: Skin blood flow, since increased flow and sweating transfer heat away from the body
Cyclists' resting body mass, since mass determines the training temperature
Total number of days since each cyclist's last race, since it sets the fluid volume
Chamber humidity at 5 min intervals only for Group A
option_rationale: Correct: a thermoregulatory effector variable directly tied to heat loss, measured in every group.
Misconception: body mass is a participant trait, not an effector of the response.
Misconception: unrelated to heat loss; confuses a scheduling detail with a physiological response.
Misconception: measuring a condition in one group only is not a consistent procedure and is not a response variable.
items.explanation_en: Heat acclimation involves effectors such as increased sweating and skin blood flow that raise heat loss and lower core temperature, a negative feedback response. Measuring skin blood flow in all groups provides direct evidence of that mechanism. Body mass and days since last race are not responses, and measuring humidity in one group only breaks consistency and measures an environmental condition, not a response.

payload.title: Effect of a CDK Inhibitor on Mitotic Index in Cultured Root-Tip Cells

stimulus.description: Table of mitotic index (percent of cells in mitosis) for cultured onion root-tip cells treated for 24 hours with four concentrations of a CDK inhibitor, with mean, 2SE, and a cell-count table for one slide.

data.table1_title: Mitotic index of cultured root-tip cells after 24 h of treatment with inhibitor R-7
table1_columns: Mean mitotic index (% of cells in mitosis)
data.table2_title: Cell counts from one slide in the 10 uM treatment
data.background: Inhibitor R-7 binds the CDK that partners with the cyclin active at the G2/M checkpoint. Cells were all drawn from the same culture, grown at 25 C, and treated for 24 h in identical medium. The control received medium plus solvent only (0 uM).

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Describe the role of the cyclin-CDK complex at the G2/M checkpoint, and identify one appropriate control for this experiment and explain its purpose. (2 points)
parts.model_answer: Cyclin-CDK complex: when cyclin levels rise and bind CDK, the active complex phosphorylates target proteins that allow the cell to pass the G2/M checkpoint and enter mitosis. Control: the 0 uM treatment (medium plus solvent only) shows the baseline mitotic index without inhibitor, so that changes can be attributed to R-7 rather than to the solvent or culture conditions.

rubric_rows.criterion: Describes cyclin-CDK role at G2/M
required_elements: Active cyclin-CDK complex (cyclin bound to CDK) triggers/permits progression from G2 into mitosis
optional_phrases: checkpoint passed only if conditions are met
common_errors: Says CDK is active at all times regardless of cyclin

rubric_rows.criterion: Identifies control and purpose
required_elements: Provides baseline for comparison so effect is due to the inhibitor
alt_solutions: Same cells with solvent only at 0 uM
common_errors: Names a treated group as the control

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Construct a graph of the data in the first table (mean mitotic index versus inhibitor concentration). Include error bars representing 2SE. (3 points)
parts.model_answer: A bar graph (or points joined by a line, acceptable because concentration is numeric) with x-axis 'Inhibitor R-7 concentration (uM)' at 0, 5, 10, 20 and y-axis 'Mean mitotic index (% of cells in mitosis)' scaled 0 to 10 or 12 in even intervals. Bars/points at 9.2, 7.1, 4.3, 1.8 with error bars of ±0.8, ±0.7, ±0.6, ±0.5 respectively.

rubric_rows.criterion: Appropriate graph type and scale
required_elements: Bar graph or line/scatter graph with concentration on x-axis and mitotic index on y-axis
Even scale intervals; y-axis starts at 0 and covers at least 0-9.2
alt_solutions: Line graph with points connected, x-axis scaled proportionally
common_errors: Uneven x scaling in a line graph

rubric_rows.criterion: Accurately plotted data with error bars
required_elements: Error bars of ±0.8, ±0.7, ±0.6, ±0.5 centered on each mean
rubric_rows.numeric_tolerance: within half a minor grid division
common_errors: Error bars plotted as full length rather than ± from mean

rubric_rows.criterion: Labeled axes with units (and legend/note that error bars are 2SE)
required_elements: x-axis label with concentration and uM
y-axis label with mitotic index and percent
common_errors: No statement of what error bars represent

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Using the cell counts for the one slide in the 10 uM treatment, calculate the mitotic index for that slide as a percent. Show your work. Round to the nearest tenth. (1 point)
parts.model_answer: Total cells = 236 + 7 + 3 + 2 + 2 = 250. Mitotic cells = 7 + 3 + 2 + 2 = 14. Mitotic index = 14/250 x 100 = 5.6%.

rubric_rows.criterion: Correct mitotic index with work
common_errors: Dividing mitotic cells by interphase cells (14/236 = 5.9%)

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Based on the data, state the relationship between inhibitor concentration and mitotic index. Then predict how the proportion of cells in G2 would differ in the 20 uM treatment compared with the control, and justify your prediction using the function of the checkpoint. (3 points)
parts.model_answer: As inhibitor concentration increases, mitotic index decreases (9.2% to 1.8%), and the 2SE bars of 0 and 20 uM do not overlap, so the decrease is meaningful. Prediction: the proportion of cells in G2 would be higher at 20 uM. Justification: R-7 blocks the CDK needed to pass the G2/M checkpoint, so cells cannot enter mitosis and accumulate in G2 (fewer cells reach mitosis, lowering the mitotic index).

rubric_rows.criterion: States inverse relationship using data
required_elements: Mitotic index decreases as concentration increases
Cites values or non-overlapping error bars
common_errors: Claims 5 and 0 uM differ significantly (error bars 7.1±0.7 and 9.2±0.8 do not overlap, so this is acceptable; but claiming no data support is an error)

rubric_rows.criterion: Predicts higher proportion in G2
required_elements: More cells in G2 at 20 uM than control
common_errors: Predicts more cells in G1 or S

rubric_rows.criterion: Justifies with checkpoint/CDK function
required_elements: Inhibited CDK prevents passage through G2/M checkpoint so cells cannot enter mitosis

payload.title: Nursery Growth-Signal Product and Root-Tip Cell Division

stimulus.description: Table of mean mitotic index (percent of 200 counted onion root-tip cells in mitosis) for four concentrations of a growth-signal product, with ±2SE.

data.title: Mitotic index of onion root-tip cells after 24 h exposure to a growth-signal product
data.context: A small plant nursery wants to decide whether buying a growth-signal product to speed root growth in cuttings is worthwhile. The owner treats onion root tips for 24 h, then stains and counts cells. Mitotic index = mitotic cells / total cells x 100. The control (0 µM) is root tips in plain water. Assume the cell cycle length is 24 h.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Construct a graph of the data in the table. Plot mean mitotic index versus product concentration, include error bars (±2SE), and label axes with units.
parts.model_answer: Line graph or scatter-with-line (or bar graph acceptable for 4 discrete concentrations; line preferred because concentration is continuous). X-axis: Concentration of growth-signal product (µM), 0-20 with even scale. Y-axis: Mean mitotic index (%), 0-30. Points: (0, 9.0), (5, 18.0), (10, 25.0), (20, 16.0). Error bars: ±2.0, ±3.2, ±4.0, ±3.6 percentage points.

rubric_rows.criterion: Appropriate graph type with correct independent variable on x-axis and dependent variable on y-axis
alt_solutions: Bar graph with concentration categories is acceptable

rubric_rows.criterion: Data points accurately plotted
required_elements: All four points plotted at 9, 18, 25, 16 (within half a minor gridline)
common_errors: Plotting mitotic cell counts instead of the mitotic index
Uneven x-axis spacing without a break

rubric_rows.criterion: Error bars correctly plotted
required_elements: Error bars of ±2.0, ±3.2, ±4.0, ±3.6 around the means
common_errors: Error bars drawn as SE rather than 2SE

rubric_rows.criterion: Axes labeled with units and scales appropriate; title or legend if needed

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the percent increase in mitotic index from the control to the 10 µM treatment, and calculate how many hours per 24 h cycle the average cell at 10 µM spends in mitosis, assuming mitotic index equals the fraction of the cycle spent in mitosis. Show your work.
parts.model_answer: Percent increase = (25.0 - 9.0)/9.0 x 100 = 177.8% (about 178%). Time in mitosis = 0.25 x 24 h = 6.0 h.

rubric_rows.criterion: Correct percent increase with work shown
Correct time in mitosis with units

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Identify the purpose of the 0 µM control and describe one variable the owner should keep constant across all treatments.
parts.model_answer: The 0 µM control (plain water) provides a baseline mitotic index in the absence of the product so changes can be attributed to the product. Keep constant: temperature, light, exposure time (24 h), onion variety, or root-tip region sampled.

rubric_rows.criterion: States control gives baseline for comparison AND names one valid constant variable
required_elements: One of: temperature, exposure time, light, onion variety, root-tip region, number of cells counted
common_errors: Naming concentration as the constant variable

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: The owner concludes that a higher concentration is always better for rapid root growth. Using the data, evaluate this claim, and explain how a signal from the product could increase the mitotic index by acting on the cell cycle.
parts.model_answer: The data do not support the claim: mitotic index rose from 9% to 25% up to 10 µM but dropped to 16% at 20 µM, so more is not always better (the 20 µM bar does not overlap 10 µM within 2SE: 25-4=21 vs 16+3.6=19.6). A signal molecule binding a receptor triggers a signal transduction pathway that activates cyclin/CDK checkpoint regulators, pushing cells past the G1/S and G2/M checkpoints so more cells enter and complete mitosis.

rubric_rows.criterion: Evaluates claim using data
required_elements: Mitotic index decreased at 20 µM relative to 10 µM (16% vs 25%)
common_errors: Saying the data support the claim

rubric_rows.criterion: Links signal transduction to cell cycle regulation
required_elements: Signal binds receptor and triggers signal transduction pathway
Activates cyclin/CDK or promotes passage through a checkpoint, increasing division
common_errors: Saying the product directly changes DNA sequence

payload.title: Cdk Inhibitor and Mitotic Index in Cultured Fibroblasts

stimulus.description: Table of mitotic index (% of cells in mitosis, mean and 2 standard errors, n = 3 plates per treatment) of cultured fibroblasts after 24 hours at five concentrations of a Cdk inhibitor, plus a no-growth-factor control.

data.setup: Fibroblasts were grown in culture dishes. Growth factor binds a receptor tyrosine kinase and triggers a signal transduction pathway that leads to synthesis of cyclins. Cells were fixed after 24 h and the percentage of cells in mitosis was counted by microscopy (500 cells per plate). The inhibitor blocks the cyclin-dependent kinase (Cdk) that drives the G2-to-M transition.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable in the experiment, and identify which treatment serves as the negative control for the effect of growth factor.
parts.model_answer: Independent variable: concentration of Cdk inhibitor. Dependent variable: mitotic index (% of cells in mitosis). The no-growth-factor, no-inhibitor dish is the negative control (it shows the baseline division rate without the growth-factor signal).

rubric_rows.criterion: Identifies both variables
required_elements: dependent variable = mitotic index / % cells in mitosis

rubric_rows.criterion: Identifies the control
required_elements: no growth factor and no inhibitor dish
alt_solutions: The 0 uM inhibitor + GF dish accepted as the comparison (positive) control only if labeled as such AND the no-GF dish is also named
common_errors: Naming the 0 uM + GF dish as the negative control

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Construct a graph of the data for the growth-factor-treated cells. Plot mean mitotic index versus inhibitor concentration, include error bars representing 2SE, and label axes with units. (Include the no-GF control as a labeled point or horizontal line.)
parts.model_answer: Line graph or scatter-with-line (or bar graph acceptable for categorical doses, but line preferred for a continuous variable) with inhibitor concentration (uM) on the x-axis (0-20) and mean mitotic index (%) on the y-axis (0-10). Points at (0,8.0), (1,6.5), (5,3.5), (10,1.8), (20,1.0) with error bars of +/-0.6, 0.5, 0.4, 0.3, 0.3. Control 1.2% shown as labeled point or dashed line.

rubric_rows.criterion: Appropriate graph type with correct axis assignment
required_elements: line/scatter graph with connected points (bar graph also accepted)
alt_solutions: bar graph with one bar per concentration

rubric_rows.criterion: Accurately plotted data with error bars
required_elements: error bars of +/-2SE at each point, correct lengths
rubric_rows.numeric_tolerance: points within half a minor gridline; error bars visibly proportional to given values

rubric_rows.criterion: Labeled axes with units, evenly scaled, and control/legend indicated

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Calculate the percent decrease in mitotic index between 0 uM and 10 uM inhibitor. Show your work.

rubric_rows.criterion: Correct percent decrease with work shown

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Describe how growth factor binding to its receptor leads to an increase in cell division, and explain why the inhibitor reduces the mitotic index even though growth factor is present.
parts.model_answer: Growth factor binds the receptor, triggering a signal transduction pathway (e.g., phosphorylation cascade) that increases cyclin production; cyclin binds Cdk to form the active complex that promotes passage through the G2/M checkpoint into mitosis. The inhibitor blocks Cdk activity downstream of the signal, so even with growth factor and cyclins present, cells cannot pass the G2/M checkpoint and fewer enter mitosis.

rubric_rows.criterion: Links receptor binding to cell cycle progression
required_elements: signal transduction pathway/cascade after receptor binding
increased cyclin (or Cdk activation) promoting progression

rubric_rows.criterion: Explains inhibitor effect
required_elements: inhibitor blocks Cdk activity downstream of the signal
cells arrested before mitosis / fail G2-M checkpoint so mitotic index falls

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: Predict the mitotic index if cells were treated with 20 uM inhibitor and no growth factor, and justify your prediction using the data.
parts.model_answer: Predicted about 1% or lower (near the 1.0-1.2% baseline). Justification: without growth factor the mitotic index is already 1.2%, and with GF the inhibitor at 20 uM lowers it to 1.0%, so both signals limit division to a similar low level; no additional large decrease is expected.

rubric_rows.criterion: Prediction with data-based justification
required_elements: prediction about 1% or lower (not higher than 1.2%)
cites 1.2% no-GF control and/or 1.0% at 20 uM
common_errors: Predicting 8% because Cdk is not needed without GF

scope_skill.notes: The primary skill is 4.A (construct a graph), but only part b is a graph task. Parts a, c, d and e are tagged 4.A but assess other skills: variable identification, calculation, mechanism explanation, and prediction. Part d is content recall on signal transduction and the cell cycle, which is not graph construction. Part a asks for the 'negative control' for the effect of growth factor, which is an experimental-design skill. Only 3 of 9 points address the target skill.

key_scoring.notes: Part a: the experiment has two manipulated factors (GF presence and inhibitor concentration). The no-GF dish also lacks the inhibitor, so it is a baseline for GF rather than a clean negative control for the inhibitor. The rubric's alt_solutions wording is convoluted. Part b: the stem says 'bar graph acceptable', but the rubric b1 and model answer prefer a line, which is inconsistent. Part b: the plotting tolerance 'half a minor gridline' is vague. Part e: the 'prediction' is not determinable from the data. The accepted range of 0-1.2% is broad, and a key with 'about 1% or lower' is a speculative expectation, not a unique answer. Part c: 77.5% is correct. The calculator metadata is inconsistent ('na' versus 'allowed').

stimulus_expression.notes: The table is complete: the columns, units, n, 2SE, setup and suggested axis ranges are all given. One flaw is that the GF + inhibitor 0 uM row is labeled with 'inhibitor', which is slightly confusing. Part b's parenthetical on the no-GF control is adequate.

distractor_explanation.notes: This is an FRQ, so there are no distractors. Common errors are listed only for some rows. Rubric rows give limited guidance on partial credit or on what is unacceptable (e.g., bar graph versus line, error bars drawn as SE rather than 2SE). The explanation of the part e justification is thin.

exam_suitability.notes: The format is plausible for an AP FRQ, but the 9 points and 22 minutes are overloaded with disparate tasks. Part c is a trivial 1-point calculation. Part e is speculative. The point allocation is poorly aligned to skill 4.A. The graph part is realistic, but part a is largely low-level recall of definitions.

review.summary: The stimulus is well specified and the graph part (b) is good. However, the bundle is only about one-third aligned to the 4.A graph-construction skill; the other parts are tagged 4.A but test other skills. The control identification in part a is muddled by the two-factor design, and the prediction in part e is under-determined. The item fails on scope/skill fit and on key/scoring clarity, and is not ready for the exam as it stands.

payload.title: Choosing a Growth-Factor Dose for a Cell-Culture Product

stimulus.description: Table of mean mitotic index (percent of cells in mitosis) of cultured cells grown with five growth-factor concentrations, with 2 standard errors, n = 5 plates per concentration.

data.title: Mitotic index of cultured fibroblasts after 24 hours
columns: Mean mitotic index (% of cells in mitosis)
data.context: A start-up sells cultured skin cells for testing cosmetics. Staff must decide how much growth factor to add to each liter of medium. Growth factor binds a receptor on the cell surface and triggers a signal transduction pathway that promotes progression from G1 into S phase. All plates started with the same number of cells from one stock, the same medium, temperature, and 24-hour incubation. The 0 ng/mL plates received medium with no growth factor. Mitotic index = (cells in mitosis / total cells counted) x 100.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable in the experiment, and identify the control group, explaining its purpose.
parts.model_answer: Independent variable: growth factor concentration. Dependent variable: mitotic index (% of cells in mitosis). Control: the 0 ng/mL plates, which give baseline division without growth factor so the effect of the growth factor can be attributed to it.

rubric_rows.criterion: Identifies both variables
required_elements: dependent variable = mitotic index / % cells in mitosis
common_errors: Naming time or cell number as the independent variable

rubric_rows.criterion: Identifies control and its purpose
required_elements: provides baseline to show change is due to growth factor
common_errors: Naming the 80 ng/mL group as the control

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Construct a graph of the data in the table. Plot mean mitotic index against growth factor concentration and include error bars representing ±2SE.
parts.model_answer: Graph type: line graph (or scatter with connecting line; bar graph also acceptable) with concentration (ng/mL) on the x-axis (0, 10, 20, 40, 80) and mean mitotic index (%) on the y-axis (0 to about 26). Points: (0, 4.0), (10, 9.0), (20, 15.0), (40, 22.0), (80, 22.5) with error bars of ±0.8, ±1.2, ±1.6, ±2.0, ±2.2. Both axes labeled with units and an appropriate evenly spaced scale.

rubric_rows.criterion: Appropriate graph type with independent variable on x-axis and dependent variable on y-axis
alt_solutions: Bar graph with one bar per concentration

rubric_rows.criterion: All five means accurately plotted with error bars of correct length
rubric_rows.numeric_tolerance: within half a small grid division
common_errors: Using 2SE as total bar length instead of ± from the mean

rubric_rows.criterion: Axes labeled with units and appropriate scale
required_elements: y-axis label with % of cells in mitosis
even scale intervals covering data range

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Calculate the percent increase in mean mitotic index from the 0 ng/mL plates to the 40 ng/mL plates.

rubric_rows.criterion: Correct percent increase
alt_solutions: 22/4 = 5.5 times the control, i.e. 450% increase

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: The company wants the cheapest medium that gives the highest division rate. Using the error bars and the cost data, state which concentration, 40 or 80 ng/mL, you recommend and justify your choice with the data.
parts.model_answer: Recommend 40 ng/mL. The means at 40 (22.0 ± 2.0) and 80 ng/mL (22.5 ± 2.2) differ by only 0.5 points, and the error bars (20.0-24.0 and 20.3-24.7) overlap, so the difference is not supported as real. Since 80 ng/mL costs $96 per liter versus $48 for 40 ng/mL, the added cost gives no clear added benefit.

rubric_rows.criterion: Uses overlapping 2SE error bars to conclude no clear difference between 40 and 80
required_elements: error bars overlap / 22.0 vs 22.5 not clearly different

rubric_rows.criterion: Recommends 40 ng/mL citing lower cost

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: The company tests a second batch of cells treated with 40 ng/mL growth factor plus a drug that blocks the growth factor receptor. Predict the mitotic index relative to 22.0 and justify your prediction in terms of signal transduction and the cell cycle.
parts.model_answer: The mitotic index would be lower, near the 0 ng/mL value (about 4%), because without receptor binding the signal transduction pathway is not triggered, so cells are not stimulated to pass the G1 checkpoint into S phase and fewer divide.

rubric_rows.criterion: Predicts decrease with justification linking blocked receptor/signal to failure to progress through the cell cycle
required_elements: blocked signal transduction so cells do not progress from G1 to S / pass checkpoint
common_errors: Saying the drug kills cells without linking to signaling

payload.title: Operator Mutation and Inducible Gene Expression in E. coli

stimulus.description: Table of mean beta-galactosidase activity (Miller units) with error bars of plus or minus 2 standard errors for wild-type and mutant E. coli grown with or without lactose.

data.title: Beta-galactosidase activity in E. coli cultures (n = 3 cultures per condition)
data.notes: Glycerol is used as the carbon source so catabolite repression by glucose is absent. Strain M1 carries a single-base substitution in the DNA sequence between the promoter and the lacZ gene; the lacI gene and the lacZ coding sequence in M1 are identical to wild type. Cultures were grown to the same optical density and assayed under identical conditions. Error bars represent mean plus or minus 2SE.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: A student claims that the lac operon in wild-type cells is induced by lactose. (i) Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable in this experiment. (ii) Identify the control group that allows the student to evaluate the effect of lactose on wild-type cells, and explain why the cultures were grown to the same optical density.
parts.model_answer: (i) Independent variable: presence of lactose (and strain). Dependent variable: beta-galactosidase activity. (ii) Control: wild-type cells grown on glycerol without lactose. Same optical density ensures equal cell numbers/growth stage so differences in activity reflect gene expression per cell rather than different amounts of cells.

rubric_rows.criterion: Correctly identifies both variables
Identifies control and justifies equal density
required_elements: Wild type without lactose is the control
Equal optical density standardizes cell number/growth so activity differences are due to treatment
common_errors: Naming mutant M1 as the control for the lactose effect in wild type

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Construct an appropriately labeled graph of the data in the table, including error bars that represent plus or minus 2SE.
parts.model_answer: Grouped (clustered) bar graph with strain on the x-axis (wild type, M1), two bars per strain (no lactose, with lactose), y-axis beta-galactosidase activity (Miller units) 0-200, bars at 2.0, 180, 165, 172 with error bars of ±0.6, ±14, ±12, ±15, and a legend.

rubric_rows.criterion: Appropriate graph type
required_elements: Bar graph (grouped by strain, with lactose conditions distinguished) for categorical data

rubric_rows.criterion: Accurately plotted data with error bars
rubric_rows.numeric_tolerance: bar heights within about 5 Miller units on a 0-200 axis

rubric_rows.criterion: Labeled axes and legend
required_elements: Y-axis labeled with quantity and units (Miller units)
Legend or labels distinguishing lactose presence/absence

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Calculate the fold increase in mean beta-galactosidase activity caused by adding lactose to wild-type cells. Show your work.
parts.model_answer: 180 / 2.0 = 90-fold increase.

rubric_rows.criterion: Correct ratio with work shown
alt_solutions: Percent increase of 8900% (89 x 100) accepted

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: A second student claims that the mutation in M1 disrupted the ability of the cell to repress transcription of lacZ in the absence of lactose. Using the data AND your knowledge of gene regulation, (i) support the claim with specific evidence from the table, and (ii) explain how a single-base substitution in the DNA between the promoter and lacZ could produce this phenotype.
parts.model_answer: (i) Without lactose, M1 has 165 Miller units compared with 2.0 in wild type, so lacZ is expressed without inducer, and lactose barely changes it (172 vs 165, overlapping error bars). (ii) The substitution likely alters the operator sequence so the repressor protein can no longer bind; RNA polymerase is not blocked, so transcription occurs constitutively.

rubric_rows.criterion: Evidence from data
required_elements: M1 without lactose 165 versus wild type 2.0
Little/no change in M1 with lactose (172 vs 165, overlapping error bars)

rubric_rows.criterion: Mechanism linking mutation to phenotype
required_elements: Repressor cannot bind, so RNA polymerase transcribes without inducer
optional_phrases: changed nucleotide sequence changes protein-binding site
common_errors: Claiming lacI protein is altered although lacI is identical to wild type
Claiming the lacZ enzyme is more active rather than more expressed

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: A third strain, M2, has a mutation in the lacI gene that changes the repressor so it still binds the operator but can no longer bind the inducer (allolactose). Predict the beta-galactosidase activity of M2 grown with lactose relative to wild type grown with lactose, and justify your prediction.
parts.model_answer: Activity would be low (near 2 Miller units, much lower than wild type with lactose at 180) because the repressor stays bound to the operator even when lactose is present, so transcription remains blocked.

rubric_rows.criterion: Correct prediction with justification
required_elements: Prediction: low activity, far below wild type with lactose
Justification: repressor cannot be inactivated by inducer and remains bound to operator, blocking transcription
common_errors: Predicting constitutive high expression like M1

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify the independent variable, the dependent variable, and one control (a strain or condition) in this experiment, and explain what the wild-type strain without inducer shows about the normal regulation of the enzyme gene.
parts.model_answer: Independent variables: bacterial strain and presence/absence of inducer. Dependent variable: enzyme activity (units/mL). Control: wild type (and/or the no-inducer cultures). Wild type without inducer has very low activity (2 units/mL), showing the gene is normally repressed (off) until the inducer is present.

parts.model_answer: Wild type: 410/2 = 205-fold. Strain M1: 402/395 = 1.02, about 1-fold (no meaningful increase).

Strain M1 fold increase

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: A manager claims: 'Strain M1 has a mutation that disrupts the repressor's ability to control the operon, so M1 makes enzyme constitutively.' Support or refute this claim using specific data from the table, and explain how the described mutation location accounts for the data.
parts.model_answer: The claim is supported. M1 makes 395 ± 30 units/mL without inducer versus 2 ± 1 in wild type, far outside overlapping error bars, so expression is no longer repressed. Adding inducer does not change M1 (402 ± 34 vs 395 ± 30, overlapping intervals). The mutation is in the operator-type sequence where the repressor binds, so the repressor cannot bind and block RNA polymerase/transcription, giving constitutive expression regardless of inducer.

rubric_rows.criterion: States a claim consistent with the data
required_elements: claim supported: M1 expresses enzyme constitutively

rubric_rows.criterion: Cites data with comparison
required_elements: 402 vs 395 with overlapping error bars or no inducer effect
common_errors: Citing only one number without comparison

rubric_rows.criterion: Links mutation location to mechanism
required_elements: repressor cannot bind mutated DNA site
transcription not blocked, so gene is on without inducer
common_errors: Saying the enzyme protein itself is altered

parts.label: d

parts.model_answer: Grouped (clustered) bar graph: x-axis strain (wild type, M1, M2); y-axis enzyme activity (units/mL) 0-450; two bars per strain (no inducer, with inducer) with legend; bars at 2, 410; 395, 402; 1, 6; error bars ±1, ±36; ±30, ±34; ±1, ±2.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: Strain M2 makes almost no enzyme even with inducer. A student concludes that M2 has a defective repressor gene. Explain why the data do not support this conclusion, and predict how the activity of a strain carrying both the M2 mutation and the M1 mutation would compare with M1 alone, with justification.
parts.model_answer: If M2 had a defective repressor, expression would be constitutive (high without inducer), but M2 is low without inducer (1 unit/mL) and still low with inducer (6 ± 2), so regulation is not the problem. The M2 mutation is in the coding sequence, producing a nonfunctional enzyme. A double mutant would transcribe the gene constitutively (M1) but make nonfunctional enzyme (M2), so activity would be low, near M2 levels, not 395.

rubric_rows.criterion: Explains why data do not support defective repressor
required_elements: defective repressor would give high activity without inducer
M2 low in both conditions, so enzyme itself is altered/nonfunctional

rubric_rows.criterion: Predicts double mutant low activity with justification
required_elements: gene transcribed constitutively but active-site mutation makes enzyme nonfunctional
common_errors: Predicting high activity because M1 turns gene on

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify the independent variable and one control group in this experiment, and explain why the glycerol-only medium is a useful comparison.
parts.model_answer: Independent variables: the bacterial strain and the sugar composition of the medium. Control: the wild-type strain (or the wild type in each medium). parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Using the data, construct an argument that the lacI gene encodes a negative regulator of the operon. Support your claim with specific values for two strains or conditions, and explain how the evidence supports the claim.
parts.model_answer: Claim: lacI encodes a repressor that blocks transcription of the lac operon when lactose is absent. Evidence: In glycerol only (no lactose), wild type has about 5 units, but Strain X (lacI mutation) has about 1080 units, a >200-fold increase, with non-overlapping 2SE intervals. Reasoning: loss of functional LacI causes expression even without inducer, so the normal LacI product must prevent transcription when lactose is absent; lactose (allolactose) relieves this repression in wild type (1200 units).

required_elements: lacI product acts as a repressor/negative regulator that keeps expression off without lactose

error intervals do not overlap / difference is large

wild type is induced by lactose, showing repression is relieved by inducer

Percent

payload.title: Reporter-Enzyme Activity in an Inducible Operon: Wild Type and Two Mutants

stimulus.description: Table of mean reporter-enzyme activity (units/mL, mean ± 2SE, n = 6 cultures per cell) for three bacterial strains grown with or without an inducer molecule.

data.title: Reporter-enzyme activity in three strains of a model bacterium
data.units: units/mL
data.background: The reporter gene is transcribed from one promoter and is controlled by a single operator sequence next to the promoter. A separate gene encodes a repressor protein that binds the operator. The inducer binds the repressor. The operator point mutant has a single-base substitution inside the operator sequence; its repressor gene is normal. The repressor-null strain has a normal operator but a deletion of the repressor gene. All cultures were grown to the same cell density in otherwise identical medium.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable in this experiment, and explain why the wild-type strain grown without inducer is a necessary comparison group.
parts.model_answer: Independent variables: strain (genotype) and presence/absence of inducer. Dependent variable: reporter-enzyme activity (units/mL). The wild type without inducer is the baseline (negative control) showing the repressed level of expression when regulation is intact, so that the effect of inducer or of each mutation can be compared against it.

rubric_rows.criterion: Correctly identifies variables
required_elements: independent variable: strain/genotype and/or inducer presence

rubric_rows.criterion: Explains the role of the wild-type uninduced baseline
required_elements: shows repressed/baseline expression with normal regulation
allows comparison to determine effect of inducer or mutation

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Construct a graph of the data in the table. Include error bars (±2SE), labeled axes with units, and a legend or labels identifying each condition.
parts.model_answer: A grouped (clustered) bar graph with strain on the x-axis (wild type, operator mutant, repressor-null) and two bars per strain (inducer absent, inducer present). The y-axis is reporter-enzyme activity (units/mL), scaled 0 to about 180. Bar heights: 4.0, 160.0; 150.0, 155.0; 148.0, 152.0. Error bars: ±0.6, ±12.0; ±10.0, ±11.0; ±9.0, ±10.0. Legend identifies inducer absent vs. present.

rubric_rows.criterion: Appropriate graph type
required_elements: bar graph (grouped by strain) comparing categorical conditions
alt_solutions: Separate bar graphs for each strain on a shared y-scale

rubric_rows.criterion: Accurately plotted data with error bars
required_elements: all six means plotted at correct heights
error bars of ±2SE drawn for each mean

rubric_rows.criterion: Labeled axes and legend
required_elements: y-axis labeled with reporter-enzyme activity and units/mL
legend or labels identifying inducer absent vs. present

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Calculate the fold induction (activity with inducer divided by activity without inducer) for the wild-type strain.

rubric_rows.criterion: Correct fold induction

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: A student claims that the operator mutation prevents the repressor from binding the operator. Support this claim with specific evidence from the data, and explain how that evidence is consistent with the claim by describing how the mutation alters regulation of transcription.
parts.model_answer: Evidence: the operator mutant has high activity without inducer (150.0 units/mL) compared with 4.0 in wild type, and inducer barely changes it (155.0; error bars overlap), similar to the repressor-null strain (148.0 and 152.0). Reasoning: the repressor gene is normal in this mutant, yet expression is constitutive, as if no repressor were present. A base substitution in the operator DNA would change the binding site so the repressor cannot bind, RNA polymerase is not blocked, and transcription occurs regardless of inducer.

rubric_rows.criterion: Cites specific data as evidence
required_elements: operator mutant activity high without inducer (about 150 vs 4.0 in wild type)
little or no response to inducer (150.0 vs 155.0, overlapping error bars) or similarity to repressor-null

rubric_rows.criterion: Links evidence to mechanism of regulation
required_elements: mutation in operator DNA prevents repressor binding even though repressor is present
transcription is no longer blocked, so expression is constitutive

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: Predict the reporter-enzyme activity without inducer in a strain with a normal operator and a point mutation in the repressor gene that changes the repressor's DNA-binding region so it cannot bind DNA. Justify your prediction.
parts.model_answer: Activity would be high (about 150 units/mL, similar to the repressor-null strain) without inducer, because a repressor that cannot bind DNA cannot block transcription, so the gene is expressed constitutively.

rubric_rows.criterion: Correct prediction with justification
required_elements: predicts high activity without inducer, similar to repressor-null/operator mutant
justifies: nonfunctional repressor cannot bind operator, so transcription is not blocked

payload.title: Altitude Training and Transcription of an Oxygen-Responsive Gene

stimulus.description: Table of relative EPO mRNA levels (mean of 4 cultures, +/-2 SE) in cultured kidney cells under four conditions and two cell lines (normal enhancer vs. enhancer with a point mutation in the activator-binding site), measured 12 hours after treatment.

data.background: Athletes who train at high altitude show increased red blood cell production. Researchers grew cultured human kidney cells at 21% O2 (normal) or 5% O2 (low) for 12 hours. Low O2 stabilizes an activator protein (HIF) that binds an enhancer near the EPO gene. One cell line carried the normal enhancer sequence; a second line carried a single-base substitution in the HIF-binding site of the enhancer. In some cultures, alpha-amanitin (an inhibitor of RNA polymerase II) was added. EPO mRNA was measured by RT-qPCR and expressed relative to the normal-enhancer cells at 21% O2 (set to 1.0).
data.units: relative units (unitless ratio to normal-enhancer cells at 21% O2)

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify the independent variable and one control group in the experiment, and explain the purpose of the control you chose.
parts.model_answer: Independent variable: oxygen level (21% vs 5%) (also acceptable: enhancer genotype or alpha-amanitin presence). Control: normal-enhancer cells at 21% O2 (baseline expression, set to 1.0), or normal-enhancer cells at 5% O2 without inhibitor. Purpose: provides a baseline/comparison so that changes in EPO mRNA can be attributed to the manipulated variable rather than other factors.

rubric_rows.criterion: Identifies a valid independent variable
required_elements: oxygen concentration (21% vs 5%), or enhancer sequence, or alpha-amanitin
alt_solutions: enhancer genotype
alpha-amanitin treatment

rubric_rows.criterion: Identifies a control group and states its purpose as a baseline for comparison
required_elements: control group named (e.g., normal enhancer at 21% O2)
purpose: baseline/comparison to attribute change to the variable
common_errors: naming a control without stating its purpose

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Using the data, calculate the fold increase in EPO mRNA caused by low oxygen in the normal-enhancer cells (5% O2 relative to 21% O2) and the fold increase in the mutant-enhancer cells. Show your work.
parts.model_answer: Normal: 9.6 / 1.0 = 9.6-fold. Mutant: 1.3 / 0.9 = about 1.4-fold (accept 1.4 to 1.5; 1.3-fold if compared with 1.0).

rubric_rows.criterion: Correct fold change for normal-enhancer cells with work
Correct fold change for mutant-enhancer cells with work

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Claim: Transcription, not mRNA stability alone or translation, is required for the low-oxygen increase in EPO mRNA. Support this claim with specific evidence from the table, and explain how the alpha-amanitin result links to the mechanism.
parts.model_answer: Evidence: with alpha-amanitin at 5% O2, EPO mRNA was 0.8, about the same as the 21% baseline (1.0, within error), compared with 9.6 without the inhibitor, even though nuclear HIF stayed high (7.8). Explanation: alpha-amanitin blocks RNA polymerase II, so new mRNA cannot be synthesized; the failure to increase shows that new transcription is needed for the rise.

rubric_rows.criterion: Cites data comparing 5% O2 with and without alpha-amanitin
Links inhibitor to blocked RNA polymerase II/new mRNA synthesis
required_elements: no new transcription so no increase in mRNA

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Using the data for the mutant-enhancer cells, argue that HIF binding to the enhancer sequence, not merely the presence of HIF in the nucleus, is required for increased EPO transcription. Then predict how EPO mRNA would change if a different mutation created a second, functional HIF-binding site in the enhancer of normal cells at 5% O2, and justify your prediction.
parts.model_answer: Evidence: mutant cells at 5% O2 have high nuclear HIF (8.2, similar to normal 8.0) but EPO mRNA only 1.3 (about baseline, 0.9 at 21%), compared with 9.6 in normal cells. So HIF presence alone is not sufficient; the intact binding site is needed for the activator to bind DNA and recruit transcription machinery. A substitution in the binding site prevents HIF-DNA binding, so transcription is not stimulated. Prediction: EPO mRNA would be higher than 9.6 (more activator bound, greater recruitment of RNA polymerase II/transcription factors). Justification: more activator binding sites increase transcription initiation.

rubric_rows.criterion: Uses data: similar nuclear HIF but low EPO mRNA in mutant vs normal at 5% O2
Explains the mutation prevents activator binding to the enhancer so transcription is not stimulated
required_elements: HIF cannot bind DNA/recruit transcription machinery

rubric_rows.criterion: Predicts increase (above normal level) with justification of additional activator binding
required_elements: reason: more activator bound increases RNA polymerase recruitment/transcription

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: The substitution in the mutant line changes one DNA base in a noncoding regulatory region. Explain why this mutation can alter the phenotype of the cells even though the amino acid sequence of the EPO protein is unchanged.
parts.model_answer: (Unscored extension.)

payload.title: Tracing Reporter Expression in a Engineered Bacterial Operon

stimulus.description: Table of mean beta-galactosidase-like reporter activity (Miller-type units, n=6 cultures per condition, mean ± 2SE) for three E. coli strains grown with or without the inducer sugar IPTG, plus a mutant-class table.

data.title: Reporter activity from an engineered operon (reporter gene lacZ-like, repressor gene R)
data.units: arbitrary activity units (AU) per OD600
rows: Point mutation in the operator DNA sequence where repressor binds
Single-base-pair substitution in repressor gene R changing one amino acid in the inducer-binding site
data.growth_conditions: Same medium, 37 C, 4 hours; inducer = 1 mM IPTG (binds repressor, not metabolized)

cross_experiment.description: Colonies from a cross of strain M2 cells x wild-type phenotypes scored on indicator plates containing inducer
cross_experiment.note: Chi-square critical value at p=0.05, df=1 is 3.84

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable in the table, and identify which strain and condition serves as the negative control for reporter expression (expression off).
parts.model_answer: Independent variables: strain (genotype) and presence/absence of inducer. Dependent variable: reporter activity (AU per OD600). The wild-type strain grown without inducer is the control showing the repressed (off) state (about 2 AU).

rubric_rows.criterion: Variables identified
Control identified
required_elements: wild type without inducer as repressed/off baseline
alt_solutions: wild type without IPTG (about 2 AU)

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the fold increase in mean reporter activity in the wild-type strain caused by the inducer. Show your work. Then state whether the difference between wild type with and without inducer is likely to be real, using the error bars.
parts.model_answer: 180 / 2 = 90-fold increase. Intervals (1.4 to 2.6 AU vs 166 to 194 AU) do not overlap, so the difference is likely real.

rubric_rows.criterion: Correct fold change
Error-bar reasoning

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Using data from the table, support the claim that the mutation in strain M1 affects the DNA binding site for the repressor rather than the inducer response. Then support a different claim for strain M2: that its mutation prevents the repressor from responding to the inducer. Cite specific values for each claim and explain, in terms of transcription regulation, the molecular reasoning.
parts.model_answer: M1: reporter is high (160 AU) even without inducer, nearly equal to induced wild type (180 AU) and not increased much by inducer (170). This constitutive expression is consistent with the repressor being unable to bind the mutated operator, so RNA polymerase can transcribe regardless of inducer. M2: expression stays low with inducer (4 AU vs 3 AU without), unlike wild type (180 AU). A repressor with an altered inducer-binding site cannot bind IPTG and change shape, so it stays bound to the operator and blocks transcription.

rubric_rows.criterion: M1 claim supported with data
required_elements: high expression without inducer (about 160 AU) compared with 2 AU in wild type

rubric_rows.criterion: M2 claim supported with data
required_elements: low expression even with inducer (about 4 AU) compared with 180 AU in wild type

rubric_rows.criterion: Molecular reasoning for both
required_elements: M1: repressor cannot bind mutated operator so transcription is not blocked
M2: repressor cannot bind inducer so stays on operator and blocks RNA polymerase

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: A cross produced 68 blue (reporter on) and 32 white colonies. Using the chi-square formula, test the hypothesis of a 3:1 ratio. State whether you reject or fail to reject the hypothesis and justify with the critical value.
parts.model_answer: Expected 75 blue, 25 white. Chi-square = (68-75)^2/75 + (32-25)^2/25 = 0.653 + 1.96 = 2.61. This is less than 3.84 (df = 1, p = 0.05), so we fail to reject the 3:1 hypothesis.

rubric_rows.criterion: Chi-square value
Conclusion with critical value

key_scoring.notes: Part d is scientifically invalid. E. coli is haploid and a 3:1 ratio has no genetic basis in a cross of M2 cells with wild type. The arithmetic (2.61 < 3.84) is correct, but the hypothesis being tested is unjustified, and the cross is also inconsistent with the earlier finding that M2 is a super-repressor with low expression. Part a asks for 'the negative control' but M2 is also off, so there is ambiguity. The calculator field is 'na' while the verification says allowed. Mean and error values are given as arrays, which is clumsy. The title has a grammar error ('a Engineered'). The expected-ratio rationale is missing. The mutant-class table mentioned in the description is not present.

distractor_explanation.notes: This is an FRQ, so there are no distractors. Common errors are listed only sparsely, and the rubric does not address alternative valid answers (for example, M2 as an additional off control, or an inducer-binding mutation versus a repressor-folding defect).

exam_suitability.notes: The question is a 9-point, 17-minute item with a contrived statistical part that would confuse students, since haploid bacteria do not give Mendelian ratios. Parts a and b are low-level. The calculator status is contradictory.

review.summary: Parts a-c are workable, but part d's 3:1 chi-square on a bacterial cross is biologically incoherent and not connected to the operon data. The stimulus wording is flawed, the calculator metadata conflicts, and the 6.B skill is only substantively assessed in part c. Reject and revise: remove or replace part d, fix the stimulus, and raise the argumentation demand in the other parts.

In strain A the enzyme gene is controlled by a promoter plus an adjacent DNA site where a repressor protein binds when galactose is absent. Cost note: each hour the enzyme is made unnecessarily slows yeast growth and wastes sugar.

Legend or labels distinguishing glucose and galactose

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the fold increase in enzyme activity in strain A when the sugar is changed from glucose to galactose.
parts.model_answer: 96 / 4 = 24-fold increase.

rubric_rows.criterion: Correct ratio

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Claim: In strain C, the enzyme gene is expressed regardless of sugar because the deleted DNA site is where a repressor normally binds. Support this claim with specific evidence from the table, and explain how the evidence connects to the claim.
parts.model_answer: In glucose, strain C has 92 units versus 4 in strain A, and its activity in glucose (92) and galactose (98) is similar within error.
