parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Using the data for strains 1 and 2 only, describe what the data show about the effect of inducer I on reporter activity in the wild type and what the R deletion does to the pattern. Then state the role of the R gene product that is best supported by these two strains.
parts.model_answer: In the wild type, activity is low without I (2 AU) and high with I (100 AU), so I induces expression about 50-fold. In the R deletion, activity is high (96 AU) with or without I, so loss of R causes constitutive expression. Therefore R encodes a repressor that blocks transcription of the reporter when I is absent.

rubric_rows.criterion: Describes both patterns with data: wild type low without I and high with I; R deletion high in both conditions.
required_elements: wild type about 2 AU without I and about 100 AU with I
R deletion about 96-98 AU in both conditions (constitutive)
common_errors: Stating only that the deletion increases expression without noting that I has no effect

rubric_rows.criterion: Identifies R product as a repressor (negative regulator) that inhibits expression in the absence of inducer, supported by high expression when R is absent.
required_elements: R product is a repressor / negative regulator
repression occurs when inducer is absent
common_errors: Saying R is required for expression

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Strain 3 carries a mutation in the operator (Oc) and strain 4 carries the R deletion plus a plasmid with a functional R gene. Support the claim that the Oc mutation affects a DNA site rather than a diffusible protein, using evidence from strains 3, 4, and 6.
parts.model_answer: Strain 4 shows a plasmid-supplied R product (diffusible) restores repression in trans: 3 AU without I versus 96 AU for the deletion. In strain 6, the same R+ plasmid and a functional chromosomal R+ are present yet expression stays high (95 AU without I), so the Oc mutation cannot be corrected by extra repressor. Strain 3 is also constitutive (94 AU) despite having R+. A defect that stays constitutive with plenty of functional repressor present acts only on the DNA to which it is linked (cis-acting), which fits a mutation in the operator binding site.

rubric_rows.criterion: Uses strain 4 (or comparison to strain 2) as evidence that R product works in trans, restoring low activity.
required_elements: strain 4 about 3 AU without I versus strain 2 about 96 AU
R product from plasmid can repress the chromosomal operon
common_errors: Using strain 4 without reference to restored repression

rubric_rows.criterion: Uses strains 3 and 6 to argue that Oc remains constitutive even with functional repressor available, so the mutation affects the DNA binding site (cis-acting) not the protein.
required_elements: strain 6 about 95 AU without I despite extra R+
conclusion that Oc is cis-acting / is a site on DNA
common_errors: Concluding Oc destroys the R protein

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Strain 5 (Rs) shows about 2 AU without I and 3 AU with I. Make a claim about how the Rs mutation changes the repressor, and support it with the data. Identify what type of mutation in the R gene (at the level of the DNA change) is consistent with the description in the table, and explain why such a change could alter the protein function.
parts.model_answer: Claim: the Rs repressor still binds the operator and represses expression but can no longer respond to inducer I. Evidence: activity stays low (2 and 3 AU, within error) with and without I, whereas wild type rises to 100 AU. A substitution (point) mutation changing one nucleotide can change a codon, replacing one amino acid in the inducer-binding site; the altered protein shape prevents inducer from binding and releasing the repressor from the operator.

rubric_rows.criterion: Claim that Rs repressor still represses but is insensitive to inducer.
common_errors: Claiming Rs is nonfunctional like the deletion

rubric_rows.criterion: Cites data: about 2 AU and 3 AU (no significant increase) versus wild-type 100 AU with I.
required_elements: strain 5 values 2 and 3 AU with overlapping error
contrast with wild type 100 AU with I

rubric_rows.criterion: Identifies a substitution (point) mutation that changes an amino acid and explains altered protein shape/binding site prevents inducer binding.
required_elements: single-nucleotide substitution changing a codon/amino acid
altered protein structure prevents inducer binding
common_errors: Describing a deletion of the gene
Saying the mutation changes the operator

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: A new strain 7 has genotype R+ O+ and carries a second mutation that deletes the reporter gene's promoter region on the chromosome. Predict reporter activity with and without inducer I, and justify your prediction using the roles of the operator, repressor, and promoter in controlling transcription.
parts.model_answer: Prediction: activity near zero (background) both with and without I. Justification: inducer removes the repressor from the operator, but RNA polymerase still needs a functional promoter to initiate transcription. Without the promoter, no transcription of the reporter occurs regardless of the repressor state, so inducer cannot restore expression.

rubric_rows.criterion: Predicts little or no reporter activity in both conditions.
required_elements: near zero/very low with I and without I
common_errors: Predicting high activity with I like wild type

rubric_rows.criterion: Justifies: promoter is required for RNA polymerase binding/initiation; inducer only relieves repression so cannot compensate for missing promoter.
required_elements: RNA polymerase needs promoter to initiate transcription
inducer only releases repressor, does not supply promoter
optional_phrases: regulation is layered on top of a functional promoter
common_errors: Saying the operator can substitute for the promoter

payload.title: Training, a Transcription Factor, and Mitochondrial Gene Expression in Muscle

stimulus.description: Table of relative mRNA levels (arbitrary units, AU) for a mitochondrial-biogenesis gene (MBG) in cultured human muscle cells under four conditions, 3 replicate cultures each, plus a mean and 2 SE column.

data.title: Relative MBG mRNA level (AU) measured by qPCR 6 h after treatment
data.setup: Cultured human muscle cells (myotubes). Contraction was mimicked by electrical pulse stimulation (EPS). Activator protein TF-A binds an enhancer upstream of MBG when phosphorylated by kinase K. Drug KI is a specific inhibitor of kinase K. Control cells received no EPS and no drug.
data.units: AU = arbitrary units relative to control mean of 1.0

extra.enhancer_mutant_experiment: In a second experiment, cells carried a point mutation in the enhancer that prevents TF-A binding. Under EPS these cells gave MBG mRNA of 1.1 AU (mean of 3 replicates, 2 SE = 0.2).
extra.chi_square_data: A researcher crossed mice heterozygous for a regulatory mutation in the MBG enhancer. Among 80 offspring, 14 showed low endurance (mutant phenotype) and 66 showed normal endurance. Expected under a 3:1 ratio: 60 normal and 20 low endurance. Critical value for chi-square at df = 1, p = 0.05 is 3.84.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify the independent variable and the control group in the first experiment, and explain the purpose of the KI-only group.
parts.model_answer: Independent variables: electrical pulse stimulation (EPS, mimicking contraction) and presence of the kinase K inhibitor KI. The control group is cells with no EPS and no drug. The KI-only group tests whether KI itself changes MBG expression independent of EPS (a drug side effect), so that the drop seen in EPS + KI can be attributed to blocking kinase K signaling.

rubric_rows.criterion: Identifies independent variable and control group
required_elements: no EPS, no drug cells as control

rubric_rows.criterion: Purpose of KI-only group
required_elements: shows KI alone does not alter MBG expression / rules out drug effect independent of EPS

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the fold increase in mean MBG mRNA in EPS-only cells relative to control cells, using the means in the table. Show your work.
parts.model_answer: 4.87 / 1.0 = approximately 4.9-fold increase.

rubric_rows.criterion: Correct ratio with work

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Using data from the table, support the claim that kinase K activity is required for the EPS-induced increase in MBG expression. Then use the enhancer-mutant result to support the claim that TF-A binding to the enhancer is also required. Explain how, in terms of transcription, phosphorylated TF-A would increase MBG mRNA.
parts.model_answer: EPS only gave a mean of 4.87 AU, but EPS + KI gave 1.30 AU, close to the control 1.0 AU (and the 2 SE intervals of EPS + KI and control overlap), so blocking kinase K prevents the increase. In enhancer-mutant cells, EPS gave only 1.1 AU versus 4.87 AU in normal cells, so TF-A binding to the enhancer is needed. Mechanism: phosphorylated TF-A binds the enhancer DNA and helps recruit RNA polymerase and other transcription factors to the MBG promoter, increasing transcription and thus mRNA.

rubric_rows.criterion: Kinase K claim supported with numbers from table
required_elements: EPS only about 4.87 vs EPS + KI about 1.30

rubric_rows.criterion: Enhancer mutant evidence
required_elements: 1.1 AU in mutant under EPS vs 4.87 AU normal

rubric_rows.criterion: Mechanism of transcriptional regulation
required_elements: increases recruitment of RNA polymerase / transcription initiation, more mRNA

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: A student concludes that EPS increases MBG expression by increasing the amount of TF-A protein. Explain why the data do not support this conclusion, and describe one additional measurement that would distinguish between more TF-A protein and more phosphorylated TF-A.
parts.model_answer: The data measure only MBG mRNA, not TF-A levels or phosphorylation, so they cannot show a change in TF-A amount; the KI result is consistent with a kinase-dependent phosphorylation step. Measure total TF-A protein and phosphorylated TF-A (for example by western blot with a total-TF-A antibody and a phospho-specific antibody) with and without EPS; unchanged total but increased phospho-TF-A would support activation by phosphorylation.

rubric_rows.criterion: Explains data do not address TF-A amount
required_elements: kinase inhibition suggests phosphorylation/activity not amount

rubric_rows.criterion: Proposes valid measurement
required_elements: measure total TF-A and phosphorylated TF-A with and without EPS

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: Using the chi-square data provided, calculate the chi-square value for the offspring counts and state whether the null hypothesis of a 3:1 ratio is rejected at p = 0.05.
parts.model_answer: chi-square = (66-60)^2/60 + (14-20)^2/20 = 0.6 + 1.8 = 2.4. Since 2.4 < 3.84, fail to reject the null hypothesis; the data are consistent with a 3:1 ratio.

rubric_rows.criterion: Correct chi-square value and decision
required_elements: 2.4 less than 3.84 so fail to reject

payload.title: Regulation of a Sugar-Utilization Operon in Bacterial Mutants

stimulus.description: Table of mean beta-galactosidase activity (Miller units) +/- 2 SE for four E. coli strains (wild type, mutant 1, mutant 2, mutant 3) grown with or without the inducer IPTG, n = 6 cultures per condition.

data.title: Beta-galactosidase activity (Miller units), mean +/- 2SE, n = 6 cultures per condition
rows: Single-base change in the repressor gene
Single-base change in the operator DNA sequence
Deletion of the promoter DNA sequence
data.background: The operon encodes beta-galactosidase, which is needed to use lactose. In the wild type, the repressor protein binds the operator and blocks transcription unless the inducer IPTG is present. IPTG binds the repressor and prevents it from binding DNA. Cultures were grown to the same density in identical medium, with or without 1 mM IPTG, and enzyme activity was assayed under identical conditions.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify the negative control and the positive control (or comparison strain) in this experiment, and explain what each allows the researchers to conclude.
parts.model_answer: The wild-type strain grown without IPTG (activity about 4) is the baseline showing the operon is normally off without the inducer. The wild-type strain with IPTG (about 820) shows the system can be induced to high expression and serves as the comparison for the mutants. The mutants are compared with these to see which regulatory component is altered.

rubric_rows.criterion: Identifies wild type without IPTG as the baseline/negative control and states what it shows
required_elements: operon is off/low expression without inducer
alt_solutions: Any strain without IPTG compared against its with-IPTG culture as its own control
common_errors: Naming a mutant as the only control

rubric_rows.criterion: Identifies wild type with IPTG as the positive control/comparison and states what it shows
required_elements: normal induced (high) expression for comparison with mutants
alt_solutions: Same conditions and culture density across strains as controlled variables
common_errors: Stating the control only keeps conditions constant without naming a strain

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Construct a graph of the data for the wild type and all three mutants, with and without IPTG, including error bars.
parts.model_answer: A grouped (clustered) bar graph with strain on the x-axis (two bars per strain: no IPTG and with IPTG), and mean beta-galactosidase activity (Miller units) on the y-axis scaled 0 to 1000. Bars plotted at 4/820, 900/880, 760/790, 3/4, with error bars of +/-2SE (1/60, 70/75, 55/65, 1/1). A legend identifies the IPTG conditions.

rubric_rows.criterion: Appropriate graph type
required_elements: grouped/clustered bar graph with categorical strains and two conditions side by side
alt_solutions: Two separate bar graphs, one for each condition, on the same y-scale

rubric_rows.criterion: Accurately plotted data with error bars
required_elements: error bars of +/-2SE on each bar
common_errors: Plotting SE as the full bar height

rubric_rows.criterion: Labeled axes with units and legend

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Calculate the fold induction (activity with IPTG divided by activity without IPTG) for the wild type. Show your work.
parts.model_answer: 820 / 4 = 205-fold induction.

rubric_rows.criterion: Correct fold induction with work
alt_solutions: about 205-fold

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Mutant 1 has a single-base change in the repressor gene and mutant 2 has a single-base change in the operator sequence. Make a claim about how each mutation affects regulation of the operon, and support each claim with specific data from the table and with reasoning about how the changed DNA alters gene expression.
parts.model_answer: Claim: both mutations cause constitutive (uninducible) expression. Mutant 1: activity is about 900 without IPTG, similar to the induced wild type (820), so the altered repressor can no longer block transcription (for example, a changed amino acid sequence prevents DNA binding), and IPTG makes no difference (880). Mutant 2: activity is 760 without IPTG, so the altered operator sequence no longer binds the repressor even though the repressor is made, and IPTG has no effect (790).

rubric_rows.criterion: Mutant 1 claim with data and mechanism
required_elements: repressor protein nonfunctional (cannot bind operator) due to altered sequence

rubric_rows.criterion: Mutant 2 claim with data and mechanism
required_elements: operator sequence changed so repressor cannot bind
common_errors: Claiming the repressor protein is nonfunctional

parts.label: e

rubric_rows.criterion: Predicts low activity with justification based on promoter function
required_elements: RNA polymerase cannot bind/initiate transcription without the promoter
common_errors: Predicting induction because IPTG is present

payload.title: Choosing a Yeast Strain for a Brewery: Regulation of the Maltose-Utilization Gene

stimulus.description: Table of mean relative mRNA level (arbitrary units) of a maltase gene in two yeast strains grown in three sugar conditions, with error as plus or minus 2 standard errors (n = 6 cultures per cell).

data.title: Relative maltase mRNA level (arbitrary units), mean ± 2SE, n = 6 cultures per cell
data.context: A small brewery compares its standard yeast strain (S) with a supplier's mutant strain (M) before buying a large batch. The wort contains both glucose and maltose early in fermentation, and only maltose later. Maltase mRNA was measured after 2 hours in each medium. Strain M has a single-base-pair change in the DNA region upstream of the maltase gene where a glucose-activated repressor protein binds; the maltase coding sequence is identical in both strains.
data.units: arbitrary units of relative mRNA
data.price_note: Strain M costs $40 more per batch than strain S.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable in this experiment, and identify which condition in strain S serves as a negative control for maltase expression.
parts.model_answer: The independent variables are the yeast strain and the sugar in the medium; the dependent variable is the relative maltase mRNA level. Strain S grown in glucose only (no maltose) serves as the negative control showing the uninduced, low level of expression.

rubric_rows.criterion: Correctly identifies variables and a valid negative control
required_elements: Independent variable: strain and/or sugar condition
Negative control: strain S in glucose only (uninduced)
alt_solutions: Strain S in glucose + maltose is also accepted as a repressed-condition control if reasoning is given
common_errors: Naming the enzyme activity rather than mRNA as the dependent variable
Naming strain M as the control

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Construct a graph of the data in the table. Include the means and error bars representing ±2SE for both strains in all three conditions.
parts.model_answer: A grouped (clustered) bar graph with sugar condition on the x-axis (glucose only, maltose only, glucose + maltose), two bars per condition (S and M) with a legend, y-axis labeled 'Relative maltase mRNA level (arbitrary units)' scaled 0 to 100, bar heights S: 4, 80, 6 and M: 70, 84, 72, with error bars of ±1, ±6, ±2 for S and ±8, ±7, ±8 for M.

rubric_rows.criterion: Appropriate graph type
required_elements: Bar graph (grouped by condition or by strain) because the independent variable is categorical

rubric_rows.criterion: Accurately plotted means with error bars
required_elements: Error bars of ±2SE on all six bars with correct lengths

rubric_rows.criterion: Labeled axes, units and legend
required_elements: Y-axis labeled with variable and units (relative mRNA, arbitrary units) with even scale
Legend or labels identifying strains S and M

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Calculate (i) the fold increase in maltase mRNA in strain S in maltose only compared with glucose only, and (ii) the percent of its maltose-only expression that strain M retains in glucose + maltose. Show your work.

rubric_rows.criterion: Fold increase in S
Percent retained in M

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: The owner claims that the mutation in strain M disrupts binding of the glucose-activated repressor to its upstream DNA site. Support this claim with specific evidence from the data, and explain how the mutation would produce this pattern at the level of transcription.
parts.model_answer: Evidence: in strain S, adding glucose to maltose lowers mRNA from 80 to 6 (about 7.5% of maltose-only level), while in strain M it stays at 72 versus 84 (about 86%), and M in glucose only (70) is far above S in glucose only (4), with non-overlapping 2SE ranges. Explanation: the base-pair change in the regulatory DNA site prevents the repressor from binding, so RNA polymerase can transcribe the maltase gene even in glucose, making expression constitutive and no longer controlled by the sugar.

rubric_rows.criterion: Cites comparative data supporting loss of glucose repression

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify the purpose of Strain D and of the without-IPTG condition for Strain A in this experiment, and explain what each allows the researchers to conclude.
parts.model_answer: Strain D (no plasmid) is a negative control showing that background beta-galactosidase activity without the reporter plasmid is essentially zero (about 2 units), so the activity in other strains is due to the plasmid lacZ. Strain A without IPTG shows the uninduced baseline with an intact repressor-operator system: expression is low (about 12 units), showing the wild-type regulatory region keeps the gene mostly off when inducer is absent.

rubric_rows.criterion: Strain D as negative control with conclusion that activity in plasmid strains comes from the plasmid reporter
required_elements: background activity ~ 0 so signal arises from plasmid lacZ

rubric_rows.criterion: Strain A without IPTG as uninduced baseline showing wild-type regulation keeps expression low
required_elements: regulatory region/repressor normally turns gene off

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Using data from the table, construct an argument that the repressor binds the operator to reduce transcription when IPTG is absent. Support your claim with specific numbers from at least two strains, and explain how the evidence links to the claim.
parts.model_answer: Claim: In the absence of inducer, the repressor binds the operator and blocks transcription of lacZ. Evidence 1: Strain A without IPTG is 12 units but rises to 1480 with IPTG, which removes the repressor from DNA, so removing repressor binding raises expression about 120-fold. Evidence 2: Strain B (operator mutation) has 1350 units without IPTG versus 12 for Strain A, so changing the operator DNA abolishes repression even with no inducer, consistent with repressor no longer recognizing the operator. (Strain C, repressor unable to bind DNA, also gives 1390 without IPTG.) Reasoning: high expression whenever the repressor cannot bind DNA (by IPTG, operator mutation, or repressor mutation) and low expression only when the repressor can bind the intact operator shows that repressor-operator binding is what reduces transcription.

required_elements: repressor protein binds the operator (DNA sequence)

rubric_rows.criterion: Links binding to blocked transcription and low activity without lactose
required_elements: bound repressor blocks/prevents transcription by RNA polymerase
no inducer (lactose) present so repressor remains bound, low enzyme

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Construct a graph of the data for all three strains in all three media, including error bars (±2SE). Use the grid description: x-axis lists media; y-axis is enzyme activity (0–110).
parts.model_answer: A grouped (clustered) bar graph with medium on the x-axis (three groups), three bars per group (WT, R, O) with a legend, y-axis 'Beta-galactosidase activity (arbitrary units)' scaled 0-110 in even increments, bars at the table means with error bars of ±2SE (e.g., WT lactose 95 with bar from 87 to 103).

required_elements: bar graph with categorical x-axis (grouped by medium or by strain)
alt_solutions: grouped by strain with bars for media

x-axis labeled; legend identifying strains (or media)

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Calculate the fold induction of beta-galactosidase activity in wild type, defined as activity in lactose only divided by activity with no sugar. Show your work.

rubric_rows.criterion: Correct ratio with work

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: The company must choose a strain for whey that may or may not contain glucose. Make a claim about which strain is best, and support it with specific data and reasoning about the molecular mechanism of each mutation (include why Strain R and Strain O differ from WT).
parts.model_answer: Claim: Strain O is best for whey of unknown glucose content. Evidence: with lactose + glucose it makes 85 ± 7 versus 6 ± 2 for WT and 8 ± 2 for R (error bars do not overlap). Reasoning: the operator mutation prevents repressor binding, so transcription is not blocked regardless of lactose; it also lacks the glucose-dependent reduction seen in WT, and R, which has a nonfunctional repressor, makes enzyme constitutively without lactose (90) but is still reduced by glucose (8) because glucose lowers activation of the operon (low cAMP/CAP activation), a separate regulatory input that the operator mutation does not alter. Because Strain O's high activity in all media is constitutive, it wastes resources when no enzyme is needed, but that is acceptable if production is the goal. (Alternative: if the whey is always glucose-free, WT, R, or O all give about 92-95, and WT is best since it is inducible.)

notes error bars do not overlap for the key comparison

rubric_rows.criterion: Mechanistic reasoning for mutations
required_elements: operator mutation prevents repressor binding so transcription occurs without regulation
repressor gene mutation yields nonfunctional repressor, so expression without lactose
glucose reduction in WT and R reflects a separate regulatory mechanism (e.g., CAP/cAMP activation) not affected by operator mutation

payload.title: Inducer-Dependent Reporter Expression in Regulatory Mutants

stimulus.description: Table of mean relative reporter units (RU) with ±2SE for four bacterial strains grown without and with an inducer molecule.

data.units: RU = relative units of reporter protein per cell, measured after 3 h of growth
data.setup: A reporter gene is placed downstream of a promoter and an adjacent operator sequence. A separate gene encodes a repressor protein that binds the operator and blocks transcription. The inducer binds the repressor. Strain R-s makes a repressor that still binds the operator but cannot bind the inducer. All strains carry the same reporter gene and promoter. Cultures were grown in the same medium at the same temperature.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify the dependent variable in this experiment, and identify which strain-condition combination serves as the baseline (control) for judging the effect of the inducer on a normally regulated gene. Explain why it is the appropriate control.
parts.model_answer: The dependent variable is reporter expression (RU of reporter protein per cell). The control is the wild-type strain without inducer (or WT with vs. without inducer), because it has an intact repressor and operator and shows the normal regulated (repressed) state against which the mutants and the inducer effect are compared.

rubric_rows.criterion: Identifies the dependent variable
common_errors: Naming the inducer or strain as the dependent variable

rubric_rows.criterion: Identifies the control and justifies it
required_elements: has intact/functional repressor and operator, so normal regulation is the comparison
alt_solutions: WT without inducer as the uninduced baseline, with WT plus inducer as the induced comparison
common_errors: Choosing a mutant strain as the control

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Construct a graph of the data in the table. Describe the graph you would draw: the type of graph, what is plotted on each axis, how the conditions are distinguished, and how the error bars are shown.
parts.model_answer: Draw a grouped (clustered) bar graph. The x-axis lists the four strains (WT, R-, O-c, R-s), each with two adjacent bars (no inducer, inducer added) distinguished by shading and a legend. The y-axis is mean reporter expression (RU), scaled 0 to about 110 with even intervals. Bar heights equal the means (2.0/96.0, 91.0/94.0, 88.0/90.0, 1.8/2.4), with error bars of +/-2SE (0.6, 8.0, 7.0, 9.0, 8.0, 7.0, 0.5, 0.7).

rubric_rows.criterion: Appropriate graph type
required_elements: bar graph with paired/grouped bars by strain and condition (categorical x-axis)
alt_solutions: Separate bar graphs for each condition, with strains on the x-axis

rubric_rows.criterion: Accurately plotted data with error bars
required_elements: bar heights match the means for all eight bars
error bars of +/-2SE drawn on each bar
common_errors: Using SE values as bar heights

rubric_rows.criterion: Labeled axes and legend
required_elements: y-axis labeled reporter expression (RU) with a uniform scale
legend or key identifying no inducer vs. inducer added

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Calculate the fold induction (expression with inducer divided by expression without inducer) for the wild-type strain. Show your work.
parts.model_answer: 96.0 RU / 2.0 RU = 48-fold induction.

rubric_rows.criterion: Correct fold induction with work shown

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: A student claims: 'The O-c mutation changes the operator so that the repressor can no longer block transcription, whereas the R-s mutation changes the repressor so that it cannot respond to the inducer.' Use the data to support this claim, and explain how each mutation produces its pattern. Then predict the reporter expression (high or low) without inducer in a strain that carries both the wild-type repressor gene and the O-c operator, and justify your prediction.
parts.model_answer: Evidence for O-c: expression is high (88.0 RU) even without inducer and is similar to the repressor deletion (91.0 RU), with overlapping error bars with inducer (90.0 RU), so the gene is expressed constitutively; an altered operator sequence prevents repressor binding, so RNA polymerase can transcribe regardless of the inducer. Evidence for R-s: expression stays low with and without inducer (1.8 and 2.4 RU, overlapping error bars), so the repressor keeps blocking transcription because it cannot bind the inducer and so is never released from the operator. Prediction: high expression without inducer, because the wild-type repressor is present but the mutated operator cannot bind it, so transcription is not blocked.

rubric_rows.criterion: Uses O-c data (with numbers) to support constitutive expression and links to altered operator preventing repressor binding
required_elements: O-c high without inducer (about 88 RU), similar to R- and not increased by inducer
mutated operator cannot bind repressor so transcription is not blocked
common_errors: Claiming the O-c mutation removes the repressor protein

rubric_rows.criterion: Uses R-s data (with numbers) to support lack of induction and links to repressor unable to bind inducer
required_elements: R-s low with and without inducer (about 2 RU), overlapping error bars
repressor cannot bind inducer so remains bound to operator and keeps blocking transcription

rubric_rows.criterion: Correct prediction with justification
required_elements: operator cannot bind the repressor even though repressor is present (cis-acting site mutation)
common_errors: Predicting low expression because a functional repressor is present

payload.title: Training Signals and a Muscle Gene Promoter

stimulus.description: Table of mean relative luciferase units (RLU) with ±2SE for muscle cells carrying a reporter gene driven by an intact or repressor-site-mutated promoter, with or without an energy-stress signal.

data.title: Reporter activity driven by the promoter of an endurance-adaptation gene in cultured muscle cells
data.background: Athletes' muscles increase expression of an endurance-adaptation gene after training. In cultured muscle cells, the gene's promoter was fused to a luciferase reporter gene. Cells were treated for 6 h with either no signal or an energy-stress signal (a molecule that rises when ATP is low during exercise). The energy-stress signal activates a cytoplasmic enzyme that leads to a transcriptional activator entering the nucleus. A repressor protein binds a DNA site in the promoter. In two of the groups, this repressor-binding site was mutated so the repressor cannot bind. Each value is the mean of n = 6 cultures.
data.units: RLU = relative luciferase units (arbitrary units, proportional to reporter transcription and translation)

graph_spec.y_axis: Mean RLU, range 0 to 500, tick interval 100

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify the condition that serves as the negative control (baseline) for this experiment, and explain why the luciferase reporter is a valid measure of the promoter's regulation of gene expression.
parts.model_answer: Condition 1 (intact promoter, no energy-stress signal) is the baseline/negative control. Luciferase activity is produced only when the promoter drives transcription and translation of the reporter gene, so RLU reflects the promoter's transcriptional activity.

rubric_rows.criterion: Identifies the control
Explains the reporter
required_elements: Reporter output depends on promoter-driven transcription/expression, so RLU reflects gene expression regulation
optional_phrases: luciferase made only if promoter is active

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the fold change in reporter activity caused by the energy-stress signal in cells with the intact promoter (condition 2 compared with condition 1).
parts.model_answer: 420 / 100 = 4.2-fold increase.

rubric_rows.criterion: Correct fold change
alt_solutions: 320% increase

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Construct a graph of the data in the table. Plot all four conditions with error bars.
parts.model_answer: Bar graph with four labeled bars at heights 100, 420, 360, 410 RLU, with error bars of ±8, ±30, ±26, ±34; y-axis Mean RLU (0-500) and x-axis conditions labeled by promoter and signal.

rubric_rows.criterion: Appropriate graph type
Accurately plotted data with error bars
Labeled axes and legend
required_elements: Y-axis labeled Mean RLU with scale

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: A student claims that the repressor normally holds the promoter's activity low in the absence of the energy-stress signal. Support this claim with specific evidence from the data, and state the reasoning that connects the evidence to the claim.
parts.model_answer: Evidence: with no signal, mutating the repressor-binding site raised RLU from 100 +/- 8 to 360 +/- 26 (error bars do not overlap). Reasoning: if the repressor cannot bind, expression rises even without the signal, so the bound repressor normally reduces transcription of the gene.

rubric_rows.criterion: Cites comparison with numbers
required_elements: Non-overlapping error bars or large increase

rubric_rows.criterion: Reasoning linking evidence to claim
required_elements: Repressor binding to the DNA site reduces transcription; loss of binding increases expression

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: Predict the reporter activity (approximately 100, 400, or 0 RLU) in cells with the intact promoter that are given the energy-stress signal but have a mutation that prevents the activator from entering the nucleus. Justify your prediction using the role of the activator in gene expression.
parts.model_answer: About 100 RLU (low), because without the activator in the nucleus it cannot bind the promoter/enhancer to promote transcription, so the signal cannot increase expression and the repressor still limits it.

rubric_rows.criterion: Prediction with justification
required_elements: Activator must be in nucleus to bind DNA and increase transcription
alt_solutions: Accept slightly above 100 if justified by incomplete block, but not 400

payload.title: Blue Light and Seedling Bending in Oat Coleoptiles

stimulus.description: Table of coleoptile bending angles after 6 hours under four treatments, 20 seedlings per treatment, with mean and 2SE values.

data.setup: Oat (Avena sativa) seedlings were grown in complete darkness for 4 days at 22 C until coleoptiles were about 2 cm tall. Seedlings were then placed in identical growth chambers (22 C, same humidity) for 6 hours. Light came from one side only. Bending angle is measured from vertical (0 degrees = straight up); positive angles mean bending toward the light source.
rows: Tip covered with opaque foil cap
data.units: degrees from vertical
data.error_bars: plus or minus 2 standard errors of the mean

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable in the comparison of treatment 1 with treatment 2.
parts.model_answer: Independent variable: presence or absence of the coleoptile tip (intact vs. tip removed). Dependent variable: coleoptile bending angle (degrees from vertical).

rubric_rows.criterion: Correctly identifies both variables
required_elements: Independent: tip present vs. removed (tip status)
common_errors: Naming blue light as the independent variable (light is constant in treatments 1 and 2)

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Identify the treatment that serves as the negative control for testing whether one-sided blue light causes bending, and explain what it controls for.
parts.model_answer: Treatment 4 (intact seedlings in darkness). It shows bending that occurs without directional light, such as spontaneous or handling-related curvature, so any bending in treatment 1 can be attributed to the light.

rubric_rows.criterion: Identifies treatment 4 and explains it shows baseline bending without the light stimulus
required_elements: Baseline/no bending without the directional light variable
optional_phrases: only the light differs from treatment 1
common_errors: Choosing treatment 2 or 3, which test the tip rather than the light

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Using the data, state which part of the seedling detects the light stimulus, and justify your claim with evidence from the table.
parts.model_answer: The tip detects the light. Covering the tip (3 degrees) or removing it (2 degrees) abolished bending compared with intact tips in blue light (38 degrees), with non-overlapping 2SE ranges, and the result is similar to darkness (1 degree).

rubric_rows.criterion: Claim that the tip senses light supported by data comparison
required_elements: Tip is the site of light detection
Cited values: 38 vs. about 3 (or 2) degrees, or non-overlap of error
optional_phrases: foil-covered tip still attached shows the tip is needed for sensing, not just for bending
common_errors: Claiming the tip removal alone shows detection (it cannot separate sensing from response); the foil treatment is needed

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: A researcher proposes testing whether the foil cap itself harms the seedlings. Describe one additional treatment that would control for this and the result that would show the cap is not harmful.
parts.model_answer: Cap the tip with a transparent (clear) cap or foil placed on the base of the seedling, leaving the tip exposed, under one-sided blue light. If bending is about 38 degrees, similar to treatment 1, the cap or foil itself does not impair bending.

rubric_rows.criterion: Describes a valid control treatment and the expected result
required_elements: Treatment keeps cap/foil present but lets tip receive light (clear cap or foil on lower region)
Bending similar to treatment 1 indicates no harmful effect
common_errors: Describing darkness with cap, which does not test the cap effect on bending

stimulus.description: Table of mean aphid counts per plant over four weeks for three treatment groups of kale plants in a market garden trial.

data.context: The owner of a small market garden is deciding whether to buy ladybug beetles (predators of aphids) instead of spraying insecticide. She sets up 12 raised beds of kale, 4 beds per treatment. Each bed has 20 plants of the same kale variety, same soil, same watering. Each bed is enclosed in mesh so insects cannot enter or leave. Every bed starts with 10 aphids per plant. Treatment A: 30 ladybugs released per bed. Treatment B: no ladybugs released, no spray. Treatment C: insecticide sprayed weekly, no ladybugs. Beds were randomly assigned to treatments. Aphids per plant were counted on 10 randomly chosen plants per bed each week and averaged per treatment.

columns: B: No ladybugs, no spray (mean aphids/plant)

data.units: aphids per plant

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable in the garden owner's trial.
parts.model_answer: Independent variable: the pest-control treatment (ladybugs released, nothing, or insecticide). Dependent variable: mean number of aphids per plant.

rubric_rows.criterion: Correctly identifies both variables
required_elements: Independent: treatment type (ladybug release vs. none vs. insecticide)
Dependent: aphid number (mean aphids per plant)
common_errors: Naming time as the independent variable only
Naming ladybug number as the dependent variable

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Identify the control group that allows the owner to determine the effect of ladybugs on aphid numbers, and explain why it is the appropriate comparison.
parts.model_answer: Treatment B (no ladybugs, no spray) is the control. It differs from Treatment A only in the absence of ladybugs, so differences in aphid numbers can be attributed to predation by ladybugs.

rubric_rows.criterion: Names no-ladybug, no-spray group and links to isolating the ladybug effect
required_elements: Differs from ladybug group only in ladybug presence / baseline aphid growth without predator
alt_solutions: Treatment C is not the correct control for ladybugs because insecticide adds a second difference
common_errors: Choosing insecticide group as the control for ladybugs

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Using the data, describe the difference in aphid population change between the ladybug treatment and the no-ladybug, no-spray treatment over the four weeks.
parts.model_answer: With ladybugs, aphids rose slightly to 14 in week 1 and then declined to 5 per plant by week 4. Without ladybugs, aphids grew rapidly from 10 to 240 per plant.

rubric_rows.criterion: Compares trends with supporting data
required_elements: Ladybug group declines or stays low (5 at week 4, or similar)
No-ladybug group increases greatly (240 at week 4, or similar)

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: The owner's neighbor suggests that the beds be left open instead of enclosed in mesh. Predict how this change would affect the validity of the experiment, and justify your prediction.
parts.model_answer: Validity would be reduced. rubric_rows.criterion: Predicts reduced validity and justifies with uncontrolled movement of organisms between beds

Justification: ladybugs/aphids/other predators could move between beds, so treatments not isolated

payload.title: Testing Competition Strength in a Two-Species Simulation

stimulus.description: Table of simulated population sizes of species X and species Y at generation 60 under four values of the competition coefficient, with all other model parameters listed.

columns: Competition coefficient a (effect of one species on the other)
data.note: Population sizes are in individuals, rounded to the nearest whole number. Each run is one simulation with a single value of a. Both species have identical r, K and starting size in every run.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: A student uses the table to test the hypothesis that stronger interspecific competition lowers the population size each species reaches. Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable in this simulation experiment.
parts.model_answer: Independent variable: the competition coefficient a. Dependent variable: population size of species X and Y at generation 60.

rubric_rows.criterion: Correctly identifies both variables
required_elements: Dependent variable = population size (of X and/or Y) at generation 60
common_errors: Naming generation number or r or K as the independent variable

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Run 1 has a = 0.0. Explain what this run represents in the experiment and why it is useful for interpreting Runs 2 through 4.
parts.model_answer: With a = 0 the species do not compete, so it is the control (baseline) run. Each species reaches its carrying capacity of 100, so reductions in Runs 2-4 can be attributed to interspecific competition.

rubric_rows.criterion: Identifies Run 1 as a no-competition control/baseline and links it to attributing the decreases to competition
required_elements: Run 1 is the control/baseline with no interspecific competition
Comparison shows lower sizes in other runs are due to competition (a)
common_errors: Saying it is a control because it has the highest value without mentioning no competition

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Identify two parameters or conditions that were held constant across all four runs, and explain why holding them constant is necessary for the conclusion about a.
parts.model_answer: Any two of: r = 0.2, K = 100 for each species, starting sizes of 10, number of generations (60). Holding them constant ensures that differences in final population size can be attributed only to a rather than to another variable.

rubric_rows.criterion: Names two constants and states they prevent confounding of the effect of a
required_elements: Two of: r, K, starting sizes, generations
Reason: so only a differs / differences are due to a, not confounding variables

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: The student now runs a fifth simulation with a = 1.5 for both species, other parameters unchanged and starting sizes still equal. Predict whether the two species will coexist at generation 60 or whether one will be eliminated, and justify your prediction using the pattern in the table. Then name one design change (not changing a) that would make the simulation test whether a small starting advantage decides the winner.
parts.model_answer: Pattern: as a increases the equal-sized populations fall (100, 67, 53, 50), approaching the point at a = 1 where each species is held at 50. With a = 1.5 (>1, interspecific competition stronger than intraspecific) coexistence is unstable; with exactly equal starts the sizes stay symmetric in the model, but any small difference would be amplified and one species would be excluded. To test a starting advantage, give one species a slightly larger starting size (e.g., 11 vs 10) while holding a and all other parameters constant.

rubric_rows.criterion: Gives a prediction consistent with the trend (reduced sizes/competitive exclusion of one species with any asymmetry) justified by the table trend, and proposes unequal starting sizes with other variables constant
required_elements: Prediction: further decline or exclusion of one species with a above 1, tied to the table trend
Design change: make starting sizes unequal while keeping a and other parameters constant
alt_solutions: Predict sizes below 50 each with symmetric starts, and note instability; design change: unequal starting sizes
common_errors: Predicting stable coexistence at higher sizes
Changing a in the design change

payload.title: Probiotic Competition Against a Gut Pathogen in Bioreactor Communities

stimulus.description: Table of mean pathogen population density (log10 CFU per mL) after 48 hours in five replicate bioreactor gut-community models under four treatments.

data.design: Each treatment used 5 identical benchtop bioreactors containing the same defined community of 6 gut bacterial species and the same nutrient broth (same glucose concentration, pH 6.8, 37 C). All bioreactors were inoculated at hour 0 with the pathogen Salmonella strain S at 5.0 log10 CFU/mL. Treatment 1: no addition. Treatment 2: add probiotic Lactobacillus strain L (6.0 log10 CFU/mL) at hour 0. Treatment 3: add heat-killed strain L (equivalent cell mass) at hour 0. Treatment 4: add strain L, but separated from the community by a membrane that lets dissolved molecules pass and blocks cells.
columns: Mean pathogen density at 48 h (log10 CFU/mL)
data.units: log10 CFU per mL
data.notes: Pathogen starting density at hour 0 was 5.0 log10 CFU/mL in all bioreactors.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable in this investigation.
parts.model_answer: Independent variable: the type of strain L addition (none, live, heat-killed, live behind membrane). Dependent variable: pathogen population density (log10 CFU/mL) at 48 hours.

rubric_rows.criterion: Correctly identifies both variables
required_elements: Independent: presence/form of strain L treatment
common_errors: Stating the dependent variable as the probiotic density

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Identify the treatment that serves as the negative control, and explain what the heat-killed strain L treatment controls for.
parts.model_answer: Treatment 1 (no addition) is the negative control. Heat-killed L controls for the effect of simply adding bacterial cell mass/nutrients/cell components (not living competition), so any reduction in pathogen density in the live treatment can be attributed to living L.

rubric_rows.criterion: Names no-addition treatment as the negative control AND states that heat-killed L controls for added cell material/biomass without live activity
required_elements: Treatment 1 no addition is negative control
Heat-killed controls for adding cell mass or dead cell components rather than live L
optional_phrases: effect of adding any bacterial material
common_errors: Saying heat-killed controls for temperature of the bioreactor

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Using the data, calculate the difference in mean pathogen density between Treatment 1 and Treatment 2 in log10 CFU/mL, and state what the Treatment 4 result suggests about how strain L reduces the pathogen.
parts.model_answer: 8.2 - 6.1 = 2.1 log10 CFU/mL lower with live L (about a 100-fold reduction). Treatment 4 (6.2, similar to Treatment 2) suggests reduction does not require direct cell contact; it is likely due to diffusible molecules or resource use affecting the shared broth, rather than direct physical interaction.

rubric_rows.criterion: Correct difference and inference from membrane treatment
required_elements: Reduction occurs without cell contact (diffusible substance or shared resource competition)
alt_solutions: About 100-fold lower, with inference of secreted inhibitory compounds

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: A researcher proposes that strain L reduces the pathogen by competing for glucose. Describe one additional treatment that would test this hypothesis, and state the result that would support it.
parts.model_answer: Add extra glucose (increase the limiting resource) to bioreactors with live L plus pathogen, compared with the standard glucose level (or use a glucose-free broth comparison). If competition for glucose is responsible, the pathogen density in live-L bioreactors with extra glucose would be higher (reduction lessened) than in live-L bioreactors with standard glucose.

rubric_rows.criterion: Proposes a treatment that manipulates glucose availability with live L and states the supporting result
required_elements: Manipulate glucose concentration with live L present
Supporting result: pathogen density higher (suppression reduced) when glucose is increased
alt_solutions: Measure glucose depletion over time and show it is faster with L and tracks pathogen decline, with a matched no-L comparison

payload.title: pH Profiles of Two Extracellular Enzymes in a Lab Assay

stimulus.description: Line graph of relative enzyme activity (percent of maximum) versus pH (2 to 10) for Enzyme P from a stomach-dwelling bacterium and Enzyme Q from a soil fungus, each assayed at 37 degrees C with excess substrate.

data.conditions: 37 degrees C, substrate in excess, same enzyme concentration for each assay
data.notes: Each point is the mean of three trials; activity measured as rate of product formation.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Using the graph, identify the optimal pH for each enzyme.
parts.model_answer: Enzyme P: pH 3. Enzyme Q: pH 7.

rubric_rows.criterion: Both optimal pH values read correctly from the graph
common_errors: Reporting the activity value (100%) instead of the pH

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain how a pH of 9 reduces the activity of Enzyme Q, in terms of enzyme structure.
parts.model_answer: At pH 9 the altered H+ concentration changes the ionization of amino acid R groups, disrupting hydrogen and ionic bonds that maintain the tertiary structure. The active site changes shape (partial denaturation) so substrate binds poorly and the rate falls.

rubric_rows.criterion: Links pH change to altered R-group charges/bonds, changing protein shape and the active site, reducing substrate binding
required_elements: pH change alters ionization/charge of R groups or disrupts H/ionic bonds
active site or protein shape changes so substrate binds less effectively
common_errors: Saying the substrate is used up
Saying the enzyme is consumed or killed without structural explanation

parts.label: c

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Using the table, identify the pH at which the enzyme has its highest activity at 25 °C, and describe how activity at 25 °C changes as pH decreases from that value to pH 4.
parts.model_answer: The optimum is pH 7. As pH decreases from 7 to 4, activity falls steadily from 100% to 5%.

rubric_rows.criterion: Identifies optimum pH 7 and describes the decrease in activity with decreasing pH.
required_elements: activity decreases as pH decreases (100% to 5%)
common_errors: Gives 150% at 40 °C as the answer to the 25 °C question
Says activity increases as pH decreases

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain, at the molecular level, why the enzyme's activity at pH 5 is lower than at pH 7.
parts.model_answer: The higher H+ concentration at pH 5 changes the ionization (charge) of amino acid R groups. This disrupts the ionic and hydrogen bonds that maintain the enzyme's three-dimensional shape, so the active site changes shape and binds lactate less effectively, lowering the reaction rate.

rubric_rows.criterion: Links pH change to altered R-group charge/bonding, changed active-site shape and reduced substrate binding.

rubric_rows.criterion: Predicts a lower reading and cites 25% (vs 100%).

parts.label: d

stimulus.description: Table of four field projects a research station wants to run this season, with the researcher-hours each requires. The station has 120 researcher-hours available.

data.title: Field projects requested at a university agricultural research station
data.units: researcher-hours per season

payload.stem: A university agricultural research station has 120 researcher-hours available this season. The table shows the researcher-hours each of four requested field projects would require. Which of the following statements best describes how the table illustrates the economic concept of scarcity?
options: The projects together require more researcher-hours than are available, so running some projects means giving up others.
The station has too few researcher-hours to complete even one of the four projects, so no project can be run.
The irrigation trial requires the most hours, so it is the project that must be given up first.
Scarcity arises because the station could get more researcher-hours if it paid higher wages, so hours are not truly limited.
Researcher-hours are scarce only if every project is run, so scarcity would disappear once any two projects are chosen.
option_rationale: Key: total requested hours (155) exceed the 120 available, so wants exceed resources and choosing requires trade-offs.
Misconception: confuses scarcity with absolute lack of resources; each project needs 50 or fewer hours, so several can be run.
Misconception: believes scarcity dictates which good is dropped based on resource use alone, ignoring opportunity cost and the value of each project.
Misconception: thinks scarcity vanishes if more resources can be obtained at some price; scarcity is about limited resources relative to wants, even when purchasable.
Misconception: thinks scarcity depends on the particular choice made; in fact the resource is limited relative to wants regardless, and any choice still forgoes the other projects.
payload.explanation_en: The projects require 40 + 35 + 50 + 30 = 155 researcher-hours, but only 120 are available. Wants exceed available resources, which is scarcity, so choosing some projects means forgoing others. The statement that no project can be run is wrong because each project needs fewer than 120 hours; scarcity does not mean having nothing. The statement that the irrigation trial must be dropped first is wrong because scarcity does not determine which project is dropped; that depends on the value of the alternatives forgone. The statement that hours are not truly limited if more could be bought is wrong because a resource is scarce whenever it is limited relative to wants, even if it can be obtained at a cost. The statement that scarcity disappears once two projects are chosen is wrong because the limit on hours persists and the unchosen projects are still forgone.

payload.stem: The Okafor household has $120 and 10 hours of free time this weekend. The table lists four activities they would all like to do. Which statement best describes how the concept of scarcity applies to this household's situation?
options: The total cost of all four activities exceeds the household's budget, so choosing some activities means giving up others.
The household can afford each activity separately, so scarcity does not apply to the household's decision.
Scarcity exists only because the restaurant dinner costs more than the other three activities.
Scarcity would disappear if the household's budget rose enough to pay for the most expensive activity.
Scarcity applies only to the money budget and not to the household's limited free time.
option_rationale: Key: total cost is $170 > $120 and total time is 16 hours > 10 hours, so limited resources relative to wants force choices and trade-offs.
Misconception: scarcity requires being unable to afford any single item; ignores that the combined wants exceed the combined resources.
Misconception: scarcity is caused by one item being expensive rather than by limited resources relative to unlimited wants.
Misconception: scarcity can be eliminated by affording one more item; wants remain greater than resources, and time still constrains.
Misconception: scarcity is only about money; time is also a scarce resource, and total time needed (16 hours) exceeds 10 hours.
payload.explanation_en: Scarcity means limited resources cannot satisfy all wants, so choices must be made. The four activities cost $70 + $50 + $30 + $20 = $170, above the $120 budget, and need 3 + 6 + 2 + 5 = 16 hours, above the 10 hours available. Therefore doing some activities requires giving up others, which is the statement about total cost exceeding the budget. The claim that each activity is affordable separately is wrong because scarcity concerns the combined wants against limited resources. The claim blaming the restaurant's high price is wrong because scarcity comes from limited resources relative to wants, not from one price. The claim that a bigger budget would end scarcity is wrong because wants would still exceed resources, and time remains limited. The claim that scarcity applies only to money is wrong because free time is also a scarce resource and also binds.

data.feasible_set: x + y <= 12, with x >= 0 and y >= 0

payload.stem: In the setup described by the stimulus, which statement best applies the economic concept of scarcity?
options: Because wants are unlimited and R is limited, the agent cannot have all of both goods, so choosing more of one means giving up some of the other.
Because R is limited, the agent should spend all of it on the good with the larger number of units, since scarcity affects only one good at a time.
Because the agent could choose any combination with x + y less than 12, scarcity does not exist unless the agent actually uses all 12 units.
Because wants are unlimited, scarcity would disappear if the agent obtained a larger fixed amount of R, such as 20 units.
Because each unit of X and Y requires one unit of R, the two goods are not scarce in relation to each other, so no trade-off arises.
option_rationale: Correct: unlimited wants meet limited resources, forcing choices and trade-offs (opportunity cost).
Misconception: scarcity applies to one good only and implies a corner choice; it actually applies to the whole resource constraint and does not dictate any particular choice.
Misconception: scarcity exists only when resources are fully used; in fact, the limit on resources exists regardless of the chosen point.
Misconception: scarcity can be eliminated by having more resources; any finite amount is still scarce when wants are unlimited.
Misconception: equal resource requirements mean no trade-off; in fact, the shared resource creates the trade-off.
payload.explanation_en: Scarcity is the condition of unlimited wants facing limited resources, which forces choices. With R = 12 shared by X and Y and wants for each unlimited, the agent cannot have everything, so more of one good means less of the other. The option about spending everything on one good is wrong because scarcity applies to the whole constraint and does not dictate a corner choice. The option saying scarcity requires using all 12 units is wrong because the limit exists regardless of which feasible point is chosen. The option saying 20 units would remove scarcity is wrong because any finite resource stock is still scarce when wants are unlimited. The option claiming equal requirements remove the trade-off is wrong because the shared resource is exactly what creates the trade-off.

payload.stem: An agricultural field station can use its fixed land, labor, and technology to produce wheat and sorghum. The table shows the maximum combinations it can produce. The station moves from point D to point E. 1.2 thousand bushels of sorghum per thousand bushels of wheat, which is higher because resources are not equally productive in both crops
24 thousand bushels of wheat per thousand bushels of sorghum, which is higher because resources are not equally productive in both crops
0.3 thousand bushels of sorghum per thousand bushels of wheat, which is the same as moving from A to B because resources are equally productive in both crops
1.5 thousand bushels of sorghum per thousand bushels of wheat, which is higher because the station is producing inefficiently at point E
option_rationale: Right number but wrong cause: the PPC is drawn with fixed technology, and a move along it does not change technology. Confuses movement along the PPC with an inward shift.
Correct: sorghum given up is 54-30=24 for 20 more wheat, so 1.2 per unit; A to B costs only 6/20=0.3, and the cost rises because resources are specialized, giving a bowed-out PPC.

Uses the A-to-B cost of 0.3 and assumes constant opportunity cost, the straight-line PPC misconception.

payload.explanation_en: From D to E, wheat rises by 20 and sorghum falls from 54 to 30, a loss of 24, so the opportunity cost is 24/20 = 1.2 thousand bushels of sorghum per thousand bushels of wheat. From A to B it is only 6/20 = 0.3. The cost rises because resources are not equally productive in both crops; as more wheat is produced, land and labor better suited to sorghum must be shifted, giving a bowed-out PPC. The option blaming deteriorating technology is wrong because the table holds technology fixed and the move is along the curve. The option stating wheat given up per sorghum reverses the goods and the units. The option claiming 0.3 and equal productivity assumes constant opportunity cost, contradicted by the data. The option giving 1.5 miscalculates by using the sorghum level at E, and wrongly calls E inefficient, though all listed points are maximum combinations.

stimulus.description: Table of five efficient production combinations of corn and soybeans for a family farm in one season, using all its land and equipment.

data.title: Family farm production possibilities (tons per season)
data.note: All points are efficient; the farm uses all of its land and equipment at each point.

payload.stem: A family farm can produce corn and soybeans with a fixed amount of land and equipment. Its production possibilities are shown in the table. As the farm moves from point A to point E, each additional 10 tons of corn costs more soybeans than the previous 10 tons. Which of the following best explains why this occurs?
options: The farm's total resources shrink as it grows more corn, so fewer soybeans can be grown at each point.
Technology for growing corn improves with each additional ton produced, which lowers the soybean output given up.
Land is not equally productive in both crops, so the land moved to corn later is increasingly better suited to soybeans.
The price of corn rises as the farm grows more of it, which raises the soybeans given up for each ton.
The farm is producing inefficiently at the points between A and E, so extra corn requires giving up more soybeans.
option_rationale: Confuses movement along the PPC with a shrinking resource base; resources are fixed and fully used at every point.
Confuses movement along the PPC with a technology change; technology would shift the curve outward, and it would not raise opportunity cost.
Correct: resources are specialized, so shifting them to corn means moving land with comparative advantage in soybeans, giving rising opportunity cost.
Introduces prices, which are not part of the PPC; opportunity cost here is measured in physical output given up, not in dollar prices.
Misreads efficient points as inefficient; the table states all points are efficient and inefficiency would not explain increasing opportunity cost.
payload.explanation_en: Opportunity cost of corn per ton is 4/10 = 0.4, 6/10 = 0.6, 10/10 = 1.0, then 20/10 = 2.0 soybeans, so it rises. This happens because resources are not equally suited to both goods: the farm first uses land best for corn, and as it expands corn it must move land that is much better at soybeans, so more soybeans are lost per ton of corn. Better corn technology is wrong because technology shifts the whole curve and would not raise the cost along it. Shrinking resources is wrong because land and equipment are fixed and fully used. Rising corn prices is wrong because the PPC measures opportunity cost in output, not dollars. Inefficiency is wrong because every point shown is efficient.

difficultyRationale: Student must read coordinates from labeled points, compute opportunity cost per unit of X for two segments (1/3 and 1), compare them, and select the correct economic explanation (increasing opportunity cost due to resources not equally suited). Concept is core Unit 1 content; arithmetic is trivial; distractors target common misconceptions (constant cost, inefficiency, total-based reasoning). Moderately more demanding than a pure definition recall item because of the graph-to-ratio-to-explanation chain.

stimulus.description: A bowed-out production possibilities curve for goods X and Y, the quarter circle x^2 + y^2 = 100, with labeled points A(0,10), B(6,8), C(8,6).

payload.stem: An economy produces only goods X and Y, and its production possibilities curve is x^2 + y^2 = 100, shown with points A (0, 10), B (6, 8), and C (8, 6). Which statement correctly explains how the opportunity cost of producing more X changes as the economy moves from A to B and then from B to C?
options: Moving from B to C costs 1 unit of Y per additional unit of X, versus 1/3 unit of Y per unit of X from A to B, because resources are not equally suited to both goods.
Moving from B to C costs 1/3 unit of Y per additional unit of X, versus 1 unit of Y per unit of X from A to B, because resources are not equally suited to both goods.
Moving from A to B and from B to C both cost 1 unit of Y per additional unit of X, because the total of X and Y produced stays constant along the curve.
Moving from B to C costs 1 unit of Y per additional unit of X, versus 1/3 unit of Y from A to B, because the economy has become less productively efficient.
Moving from A to B costs 2 units of Y in total and from B to C costs 2 units of Y in total, so the opportunity cost of X is constant.
option_rationale: Correct: computes 2/2 = 1 for B to C and 2/6 = 1/3 for A to B, and attributes the rise to imperfectly adaptable resources (increasing opportunity cost).
Reverses the two ratios, a misconception that a bowed-out curve has decreasing opportunity cost.
Confuses a bowed-out curve with a straight-line PPC and treats the opportunity cost as constant; X+Y is not constant on this curve.
The numbers are right, but it wrongly says that moving along the PPC reduces efficiency; every point on the curve is efficient.
Looks only at the total Y given up, ignoring that the X gained differs (6 vs 2), so it wrongly concludes the cost is constant.
payload.explanation_en: From A to B, X rises by 6 while Y falls by 2, so the opportunity cost is 2/6 = 1/3 Y per X. From B to C, X rises by 2 while Y falls by 2, so the cost is 1 Y per X. The opportunity cost rises as more X is produced, which is what a bowed-out PPC shows, and it occurs because resources are not equally productive in both goods, so the best X-suited resources are used first. The option with reversed ratios implies decreasing cost, which a bowed-out curve contradicts. The option claiming a constant total of X and Y mistakes the curve for a straight line, and the sum is not constant here (8 at A... 10, 14, 14 at B and C but 10 at A). The option blaming lost efficiency is wrong because all points on the curve are productively efficient. The option comparing total Y lost ignores the different amounts of X gained, so it does not give a per-unit cost.

payload.stem: A sports medicine clinic uses all of its staff and equipment efficiently to produce fitness assessments and therapy sessions. The table shows the combinations it can produce each week. As the clinic moves from combination A to B to C to D to E, the number of therapy sessions given up for each additional 10 assessments rises. Which of the following best explains this pattern?
options: The clinic is operating inside its production possibilities curve, so some resources are idle and must be reallocated at higher cost.
Staff and equipment are not equally well suited to both activities, so resources moved into assessments become progressively less productive there.
Technological improvement in therapy has shifted the production possibilities curve outward, raising the cost of assessments.
Resources are perfectly adaptable between the two activities, so each extra assessment costs the same number of therapy sessions.
Demand for fitness assessments is rising, which raises the price and therefore the opportunity cost of producing them.
option_rationale: Misconception: confuses efficient points on the curve with inefficiency inside it; the stem says resources are used efficiently.
Correct: specialized resources yield increasing opportunity cost, a bowed-out PPC.
Misconception: confuses a shift of the PPC with movement along it; no change in technology occurs.
Misconception: describes constant opportunity cost (straight-line PPC), which contradicts the table's rising cost.
Misconception: attributes opportunity cost to demand and price rather than resource productivity trade-offs.
payload.explanation_en: Giving up 4, 8, 12, then 20 therapy sessions for each additional 10 assessments shows increasing opportunity cost. This occurs because resources are not equally suited to both uses: the first resources moved are best at assessments, and later ones are better at therapy, so more therapy is lost per assessment gained. The idle-resources explanation is wrong because all points are efficient and lie on the curve. The technology explanation is wrong because that would shift the curve, while this is movement along it. The perfectly adaptable resources explanation would give a constant cost, which the table contradicts. The rising demand explanation is wrong because the PPC reflects production trade-offs, not prices or demand.

data.title: Maximum daily output if all plots are devoted to one crop

payload.stem: Two agricultural field stations, Alder and Birch, can each grow wheat and soybeans. The table shows the maximum daily output of each crop if a station devotes all of its plots to that crop. Opportunity costs are constant. Which of the following correctly identifies the comparative advantage based on the data?
options: Alder has the comparative advantage in soybeans, because it gives up 3 bushels of wheat per bushel of soybeans while Birch gives up 9.
Alder has the comparative advantage in both crops, because it can produce more of each crop per day than Birch.
Birch has the comparative advantage in soybeans, because it gives up only 1/9 bushel of soybeans per bushel of wheat.
Alder has the comparative advantage in wheat, because it can produce 60 bushels of wheat, more than Birch's 45.
Neither station has a comparative advantage, because Alder is more productive than Birch in both crops.
option_rationale: Correct: opportunity cost of a soybean is 60/20 = 3 wheat for Alder and 45/5 = 9 wheat for Birch; the lower cost means Alder's comparative advantage is soybeans.
Confuses absolute advantage with comparative advantage; one station cannot have the lower opportunity cost in both goods.
Misreads the ratio: 1/9 soybean is Birch's cost of producing wheat, which indicates Birch's advantage in wheat, not soybeans.
Uses larger output (absolute advantage) as the criterion; Alder's opportunity cost of wheat (1/3 soybean) is higher than Birch's (1/9).
Believes that absolute advantage in both goods eliminates comparative advantage; opportunity costs still differ, so each station has one.
payload.explanation_en: Compute opportunity costs. Alder gives up 60/20 = 3 bushels of wheat per bushel of soybeans; Birch gives up 45/5 = 9 bushels of wheat. Alder's lower cost gives it the comparative advantage in soybeans (and Birch has it in wheat: 1/9 versus 1/3 soybean per wheat). The claim that Alder has the advantage in both crops is wrong because it confuses absolute with comparative advantage, and comparative advantage cannot belong to one party in both goods. The claim that Birch has the advantage in soybeans misattributes the 1/9 figure, which is Birch's cost of wheat. The claim that Alder has the advantage in wheat uses raw output, but Alder's wheat cost of 1/3 soybean exceeds Birch's 1/9. The claim that there is no comparative advantage is wrong because opportunity costs differ, so each station has a comparative advantage in one good.

payload.stem: Dana and Eli share a kitchen and each can spend an hour making only loaves of bread, only jars of jam, or a combination at a constant trade-off, as shown in the table. Based on the data, which statement correctly identifies how they should specialize and why?
options: Dana should specialize in bread and Eli in jam, because Dana produces more loaves per hour than Eli does.
Dana should specialize in both goods and Eli in neither, because Dana can produce more of each good per hour.
Dana should specialize in jam and Eli in bread, because Eli gives up 1 jar per loaf while Dana gives up 2 jars per loaf.
Dana should specialize in bread and Eli in jam, because Eli gives up 1 loaf per jar while Dana gives up 2 loaves per jar.
Dana and Eli cannot gain from specializing, because Dana has an absolute advantage in producing both goods.
option_rationale: Compares raw output rather than opportunity cost; Dana's higher bread output does not imply a lower opportunity cost.
Confuses absolute advantage with comparative advantage; ignores that one person cannot have a comparative advantage in both goods.
Correct: Eli's opportunity cost of bread (1 jar) is below Dana's (2 jars), so Eli has the comparative advantage in bread and Dana in jam (0.5 loaf vs 1 loaf).
Inverts the opportunity costs: Dana gives up 0.5 loaf per jar and Eli gives up 1 loaf per jar, so Dana, not Eli, has the lower cost of jam.
Believes trade requires that one party be better at nothing; gains from trade depend on differing opportunity costs, not absolute advantage.
payload.explanation_en: Opportunity cost of one loaf: Dana gives up 12/6 = 2 jars, Eli gives up 4/4 = 1 jar. Eli has the lower opportunity cost of bread, so Eli has the comparative advantage in bread. Opportunity cost of one jar: Dana gives up 6/12 = 0.5 loaf, Eli gives up 1 loaf, so Dana has the comparative advantage in jam. Specializing accordingly (Dana in jam, Eli in bread) and trading yields gains. The option saying Dana should make both goods confuses absolute with comparative advantage. The option based on Dana's higher loaf output compares quantities instead of opportunity costs. The option saying Eli gives up 1 loaf per jar versus 2 for Dana inverts the ratios (Dana's cost of jam is actually lower). The option denying gains from trade is wrong because opportunity costs differ, so mutually beneficial trade exists.

payload.stem: Alpha and Beta can trade, with each producer specializing in the good for which it has the comparative advantage. Based on the table, which of the following exchange rates would make BOTH producers better off than producing each good on their own?
options: Alpha trades 1 unit of Y to Beta in exchange for 1.5 units of X
Alpha trades 1 unit of Y to Beta in exchange for 2 units of X
Alpha trades 1 unit of Y to Beta in exchange for 4 units of X
Alpha trades 1 unit of Y to Beta in exchange for 3 units of X
Alpha trades 1 unit of Y to Beta in exchange for 5 units of X

Equal to Alpha's opportunity cost of Y; Alpha gains nothing. Student treats the boundary as a gain.
Equal to Beta's opportunity cost of Y; Beta gains nothing. Student treats the boundary as a gain.
Correct: lies strictly between Alpha's opportunity cost (2 X per Y) and Beta's (4 X per Y), so both gain.
Above Beta's opportunity cost of 4 X per Y, so Beta would pay more than producing Y itself; student thinks Alpha, with absolute advantage, should get the best terms.
payload.explanation_en: Alpha's opportunity cost of 1 Y is 24/12 = 2 X; Beta's is 20/5 = 4 X. Alpha therefore has the comparative advantage in Y (and Beta in X, since 0.25 Y < 0.5 Y), even though Alpha has the absolute advantage in both goods. Alpha specializes in Y and Beta in X. Both gain only if the price of 1 Y is strictly between 2 X and 4 X, and 3 X per Y is the only option in that range. 1.5 X leaves Alpha worse off than making X itself. 2 X leaves Alpha no better off. 4 X leaves Beta no better off. 5 X makes Beta worse off than producing Y itself.

The option assigning scans to Beta reverses the opportunity costs. The 1.5-visit price is below Alpha's own cost of 2 visits, so Alpha would be worse off.
